docs.title: What is courtpy?
docs.text:
courtpy collects court opinions, turns them into data, and analyzes them. It is designed for empirical legal research, where the data has to be explained and the results reproduced. You don't need to know how to code to use courtpy. Everything is described in a simple settings files and parsing instructions are located in CSV files (of which many are included out of the box). But if you do code, courtpy is highly extensible to allow easy data munging, creation of new fields, and wrapping custom tools.

  • Collect opinions from CourtListener, from its free bulk data or its API, or use opinions you downloaded from Lexis-Nexis.
  • Parse them into a table, one row for each case, with rules written in spreadsheets (CSV files) that anyone can read and change: the parties and their roles, the court, the judges, the disposition, the issues discussed, the citations, and more.
  • Study the judges on each case, with integration of the Federal Judicial Center's biographical data and Judicial Common Space Scores (from fjc-biographies and judicial-common-space). Data about the overall political and judicial context can also be easily added, including Martin-Quinn scores, NOMINATE scores of Congress, the Supreme Court Database, and the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database of appeals.
  • Analyze the data with amos (which is built into courtpy), which compares models, preprocessing, and statistical methods, and records everything needed to reproduce the results.

docs.title: Why use courtpy?
docs.text:
• Transparent. What courtpy finds in an opinion comes from rules in CSV files, not from code, so a study's methods can be read, reported, and changed by anyone who can use a spreadsheet. The rules are part of the study, so others can check them.
  • Reproducible. A whole study (which cases, how they were parsed and coded, and how they were analyzed) fits in one settings file, and amos records every step and the version of every package.

docs.title: Techniques and datasets
docs.text:
courtpy is built on amos. A study is an amos project, described in one settings file that names techniques in steps of the project's workers. courtpy adds these techniques to those of amos, and a settings file can name them like any other:

StageStepsTechniques wranglerLoadersdownload_biographies, download_idb, download_jcs, download_politics, download_scdb, load_cases, load_court_listener, load_idb, load_lexis_nexis, load_politics, load_roster, load_scdb Parsersparse_agencies, parse_all, parse_citations, parse_civil, parse_constitutional, parse_criminal, parse_federal, parse_general, parse_header, parse_lexis_nexis, parse_review Cleanersdrop_text_columns Mungerscode_case_type, code_outcome, code_panels, code_parties, split_values, tidy_cases Mergersadd_biography, add_circuit, add_court_scores, add_executive, add_high_court, add_idb, add_jcs, add_judge_scores, add_legislature, add_scdb Shaperscases_to_case_types, cases_to_courts, cases_to_dockets, cases_to_judges, cases_to_party_types, cases_to_votes, dockets_to_cases, dockets_to_votes, votes_to_cases explorerDescriberscompare_with_idb criticEvaluatorsaudit_coverage, audit_parsing, audit_random_assignment, validate_coding Infererspanel_effects artistPlotscases_over_time, court_rates, idb_confusion_matrices, idb_missing_differences, issues_over_time, judge_network, lower_court_rates, panel_composition, trends_by_administration

Each of courtpy's datasets is an amos.Dataset whose rows are one kind of thing. The loaders make Cases, and the shapers turn one kind into another:

Dataset One row for each Made by Cases Case, with its information and the text of its sections. the loaders, votes_to_cases, dockets_to_cases Dockets Docket number of each case (a case that consolidated several appeals has a row for each), with the case's columns. cases_to_dockets Votes Judge on each case (or on each docket), with the case's columns and the judge's vote. cases_to_votes, dockets_to_votes Judges Judge, with what is known about the judge and summaries of the judge's votes. cases_to_judges Courts Court, with summaries of its cases and judges. cases_to_courts CaseTypes Case type (such as criminal, civil, tort, or contract), with summaries of its cases. cases_to_case_types PartyTypes Party type, with summaries of the cases of parties of that type. cases_to_party_types

Cases, Dockets, and Votes can be made from each other. The others summarize many cases and keep nothing about any one of them (such as its docket number or date), so a researcher can see, for example, the mix of case types that each court decides, but there is no going back. Every dataset can be saved and loaded whole (with save and load), as amos's save_data saves it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
courtpy requires Python 3.11 or later. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Extracting cases from CourtListener's bulk data needs a good connection and room for the bulk files (about 63 GB for the opinions, clusters, and dockets), unless they are streamed. Downloading with the API needs a free CourtListener account.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install courtpy, use pip:

pip install courtpy

To install the latest development version from GitHub instead:

pip install git+https://github.com/WithPrecedent/courtpy

To work on courtpy itself, see the contribution guide.

docs.title: Collecting opinions from CourtListener
docs.text:
CourtListener offers its opinions in two ways, and courtpy uses both. Both save each case as a JSON file in a folder named for its court (such as courtlistener/ca1/4567890.json), and the parser reads them the same way.

The bulk data is the whole CourtListener database, published as compressed CSV files every three months. It needs no API key and has no limits, so it is the best way to collect many cases. The files are large (the opinions file is more than 50 GB), so extracting cases takes a few hours. The files are kept outside your project so that they can be used again:

import courtpy

courtpy.BulkData().extract(
    courts = "federal_circuits",
    start_date = "2019-01-01",
    end_date = "2019-12-31",
    folder = "courtlistener")

The API is best for small or very recent sets of cases. It needs an API key: sign in to CourtListener and open the "API" page of your profile. A free account can make 5 requests a minute, 50 an hour, and 125 a day (as of 2026). courtpy asks for 20 cases at a time, waits when CourtListener asks it to, and saves its place, so a download stopped by the daily limit resumes where it stopped when it is run again:

courtpy.CourtListener().download("ca1", "2026-09-01", "2026-09-30", "courtlistener")

Courts are named by their CourtListener ids (such as ca1, cadc, cafc, and scotus) or by groups: federal_appellate, federal_circuits, and scotus.

Store your API key once with courtpy key set. See Keeping your API key secret for where it is kept and how courtpy finds it.

docs.title: Using opinions from Lexis-Nexis
docs.text:
Lexis-Nexis downloads many cases into one text file. Divide such files into one file for each case, and then parse them as the source "lexis_nexis":

courtpy.lexis.split("downloads", folder = "lexis_nexis")
table = courtpy.parse("lexis_nexis", source = "lexis_nexis")

docs.title: Parsing and coding
docs.text:
courtpy.parse reads a folder of saved cases and returns a pandas.DataFrame, one row for each case, labeled by its id. courtpy.code codes it and makes it Cases:

table = courtpy.parse("courtlistener")
cases = courtpy.code(table)  # parties, case types, and outcomes
cases.save("cases.csv")  # and the whole dataset in "cases.joblib"
cases = courtpy.Cases.load("cases.csv")

The rules are in the CSV files in courtpy's instructions folder, with a guide to writing your own. For example, the rules for federal cases may make more than 250 variables, including:

Variables Meaning party1, party2 The parties on each side of "v." party1_appellant, party2_respondent, party1_united_states, ... Each party's role, and whether it is the United States. court_num, court_name courtpy's number and name for the court in "instructions/federal/courts.csv" (such as 10 and "tenth_circuit"): for a court of appeals, its number is its circuit (1 to 11, 12 for the D.C. Circuit, 13 for the Federal Circuit), and 99 for the Supreme Court. lower_court_num, lower_court_name The same for the court whose decision is reviewed (such as "district_of_colorado"), from the history (or CourtListener's docket). Missing for a review of an agency. panel_judges, panel_size, author, concurring, dissenting The judges. disposition_reverse, decision_reverse, opinion_reverse, ... The disposition: from the header, from the decision that the opinion states ("AFFIRMED."), and from the opinion's words anywhere. party1_agencies, party2_agencies, history_agencies The federal agencies that each party and the history name, separated by "; " (from "instructions/federal/agencies.csv"). agencies Every federal agency that the case names, separated by "; " (such as "Internal Revenue Service; United States Tax Court"). civil_..., constitutional_..., criminal_..., procedure_..., standard_... Issues discussed in the opinion (such as criminal_firearm, civil_titlevii, and standard_de_novo). review_district, review_agency, review_immigration, district_judges The kind of review, and the district judge of an appeal from a district court. citations_case, citations_statute, ... Citations in the opinion. published, year, date_filed, word_count Other information.

The coders (which are amos techniques) add each party's role in the appeal and in the case (such as party2_criminal_defendant), the case types (type_criminal, type_civil, and one for each other prefix of the civil, criminal, and constitutional rules, such as type_tort and type_contract), and the outcomes: outcome_reversal, outcome_party1_won, outcome_criminal_defendant_won, and others.

docs.title: Adding the judges and the politics of the day
docs.text:
The rules find the judges' names as an opinion writes them ("LYNCH"). To study the judges, make a roster once from the Federal Judicial Center's biographical directory (three small files, which fjc-biographies downloads and parses), and more coders can use it. jcs = True adds each judge's Judicial Common Space score, computed by judicial-common-space:

courtpy.judges.Roster.from_fjc(jcs = True).save()
votes = courtpy.code(table, [
    "code_parties", "code_case_type", "code_outcome", "code_panels",
    "add_executive", "add_legislature", "add_circuit", "cases_to_votes"])

Cases, judges, years, and other researchers' data are tables whose rows are different things, so these coders are the mergers and shapers of amos: a merger adds the columns of another table to the rows that it matches, without ever adding or losing a row, and records how many rows it matched.

Coder Adds add_biography What the roster says about each judge. In Cases, the columns are numbered by each judge's seat on the panel (judge_name1, judge_party1, judge_woman1, ..., judge_name2, ...); in Votes, each row has its judge's (judge_party, ...). A function can take the place of the roster. add_jcs Each judge's Judicial Common Space score, numbered in the same way (judge_jcs1, ...). code_panels The judges of each panel who were found in the roster (panel_names and panel_found, and each judge's Federal Judicial Center name and number in judge_name1 and judge_nid1, judge_name2 and judge_nid2, and so on) and the panel's composition, such as panel_party (the mean party of the presidents who appointed its judges, from -1 for Democrats to 1 for Republicans), panel_woman, panel_age, and panel_prosecutor. add_executive The executive (president for federal cases) on the day the case was decided (executive_name) and their political party (executive_ideology, -1 or 1). add_legislature For federal cases, the median NOMINATE score of each chamber of the Congress then sitting (senate_ideology and house_ideology). add_high_court For federal cases, Martin-Quinn score of the median justice in the Supreme Court's term then sitting (high_court_ideology). add_circuit The makeup of the whole circuit on the day the case was decided (for a district court, the circuit that hears its appeals): the median and total of the parties of the presidents who appointed its active judges (circuit_median_party, circuit_total_party) and of their Judicial Common Space scores (circuit_median_jcs, circuit_total_jcs). Senior judges, who do not sit en banc, are left out. add_judge_scores, add_court_scores Behavioral scores of each judge or court computed from training data (such as a table of Judges or Courts made from the training cases), matched by the judge's or court's number. cases_to_votes Votes: a table with one row for each judge on each case, with the judge's attributes (judge_party, ...), the other judges' (colleagues_party, ...), and the judge's vote (vote_reversal, the outcome or its opposite for a judge who dissented). votes_to_cases Undoes cases_to_votes: Votes become Cases again. cases_to_judges Judges: a table with one row for each judge, with how many cases the judge decided (cases), the judge's attributes, and the shares of the judge's votes (vote_reversal, judge_dissented, ...) and of the judge's cases of each type (type_criminal, ...). cases_to_courts, cases_to_case_types, cases_to_party_types Courts, CaseTypes, and PartyTypes: a row for each court, case type, or party type, with the number of cases and the means of their columns. add_scdb For cases of the Supreme Court, the coding of the Supreme Court Database, such as scdb_issueArea, scdb_decisionDirection, and scdb_partyWinning. cases_to_dockets, dockets_to_cases, dockets_to_votes Dockets: a row for each docket number of each case, as records kept by docket need, and Cases or Votes (a row for each judge on each docket) made from them. add_idb For cases of the courts of appeals (best added to Dockets, so each docket of a consolidated case gets its own record), the record of the appeal in the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database, which fjc-idb reads, such as idb_appeal_type, idb_judgment_date, idb_pro_se_party, and idb_district_judge (and, if asked, the district court's record of the case appealed).

compare_with_idb (an explorer) checks a study against the Integrated Database. It compares the study's cases as Dockets, since the database has a record for each docket. One table shows how often the variables both have (such as whether an appeal is criminal, was reversed, or was published) agree, with the disagreements in each direction and Cohen's kappa. A second table compares the database's appeals that the study lacks with those it has, by circuit or district, with a test of each difference. A study never has every appeal, so what matters is whether the missing ones differ, such as in how often they were reversed. idb_confusion_matrices and idb_missing_differences draw the two tables.

courtpy downloads the scores and the databases from their sources the first time they are needed. To study one of these tables by itself (such as each justice's vote in each case), start with its loader instead: load_roster, load_scdb, load_idb, or load_politics, or their "download_" twins (download_biographies, download_scdb, download_idb, download_politics, and download_jcs), which download the latest files first. See examples/cases_to_votes.ini for a study of judges' votes.

docs.title: Describing a whole study in one file
docs.text:
A study is an amos project, described in one settings file. courtpy adds loaders to amos: load_court_listener, load_lexis_nexis, and load_cases. Named first in the wrangler, a loader collects the cases (downloading them, if asked), parses them, and codes them, so the project needs no other data. See examples/federal_appeals.ini:

[general]
seed = 43
label = outcome_reversal

[files]
input_folder = data
interim_folder = data

[appeals_project]
appeals_workers = wrangler, analyst, critic

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, filter_rows, keep_columns, drop_missing

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = courtlistener
download = bulk
courts = federal_circuits
start_date = 2019-01-01
end_date = 2019-12-31
save = cases.csv
reuse = true

[analyst]
design = experiment
criterion = roc_auc
steps = split, model
split_techniques = stratified
model_techniques = baseline, logit, random_forest

[critic]
techniques = scorecard

The loader finds (and saves) the cases in the input folder ("data") and saves the coded table in the interim folder, with the whole dataset beside it ("cases.joblib"). With reuse = true, later runs load that dataset instead of parsing the cases again.

Run it from a terminal with courtpy run federal_appeals.ini --export, or in Python:

project = courtpy.Project.create("federal_appeals.ini")
print(project.result.tables["scorecard"])
project.export()

courtpy.Project is amos.Project, so everything in the amos documentation works.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Does courtpy key set, show, delete Manages your CourtListener API key. courtpy download bulk --courts ca1 --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-12-31 Extracts cases from the bulk data. courtpy download api --courts ca1 --start 2026-09-01 Downloads cases with the API. courtpy download bulk --help Lists the options of one way to download. courtpy split FILES --folder lexis_nexis Divides Lexis-Nexis files of many cases. courtpy parse FOLDER --output cases.csv Parses and codes saved cases into a table. courtpy rules my_rules.csv Checks a file of rules and lists the variables it makes. courtpy run study.ini --export Runs a whole study. courtpy judges Makes the roster of judges from the Federal Judicial Center's files.

Add --help to any command for its options. See the documentation for a tutorial, the advanced user guide, a guide to writing rules, a guide to building a study on courtpy, a catalog of its techniques and variables, and recipes.

docs.text: Contributors are always welcome. Feel free to grab an issue to work on or make a suggested improvement. If you wish to contribute, please read the Contribution Guide and Code of Conduct.

docs.text: The tutorial shows how to build a study. This guide describes how courtpy works and everything you can configure.

docs.title: How the pieces fit together
docs.text:
CourtListener ──BulkData / CourtListener──▶ saved cases ──read──▶ Case ──Parser──▶ case table ──coders──▶ amos.Dataset ──amos.Project──▶ results
Lexis-Nexis   ──lexis.split──────────────▶ (JSON or text)        (sections   (rulebooks)  (one row      (parties,                   (models, tables,
                                                                   of text)                 per case)     outcomes)                   figures, report)

In a project, a loader (such as load_court_listener) does every step before amos.Dataset as the first technique of the wrangler.

courtpy's modules are in four folders, as amos keeps its modules in a folder for each stage: sources (where cases come from), wrangler (courtpy's steps of the amos wrangler), references (tables that describe something other than cases), and core (what the others share). Each module can also be imported from courtpy itself (such as courtpy.judges for courtpy.references.judges).

Folder Module Contents sources courtpy.bulk BulkData, which extracts cases from CourtListener's bulk data. sources courtpy.courtlistener CourtListener, a client for the REST API, and read_case, which reads a saved CourtListener case. sources courtpy.lexis split and read_case for Lexis-Nexis text files. wrangler courtpy.rules courtpy's rulebooks (RULEBOOKS, such as "federal"), which are amos rulebooks (amos.parsers.ParseAll) of the CSV files of rules, and register_rulebooks, which makes rulebooks of a study's own folders of rules. wrangler courtpy.parsers Parser and parse, which turn saved cases into a table, and the parse_all technique (ParseAll), which parses loaded cases again from their kept text. wrangler courtpy.coders The coders, which are amos techniques (including tidy_cases, which gives columns with missing values the right types), and code, which applies them. wrangler courtpy.shapers cases_to_dockets and dockets_to_cases, which make a row for each docket number of each case and make cases of them again, cases_to_courts, cases_to_case_types, and cases_to_party_types, which summarize cases by court, case type, and party type, and summarize, which they share with cases_to_judges. wrangler courtpy.loaders The loaders, which are amos techniques that collect, parse, and code cases in a project, and ReferenceLoader, the base of the techniques that load other tables (see Reference tables). artist courtpy.plots The plots, which are amos plots: court_rates, cases_over_time, issues_over_time, panel_composition, lower_court_rates, trends_by_administration, and judge_network (see Figures and checks). critic courtpy.audits The evaluators that check court data: audit_random_assignment, audit_parsing, audit_coverage, and validate_coding. critic courtpy.inferers panel_effects, which estimates the effect of a judge's colleagues on the judge's vote. references courtpy.judges Roster, which matches the names in opinions to judges (from a roster that fjc-biographies makes), and the add_biography, add_jcs, add_circuit, code_panels, cases_to_votes, dockets_to_votes, votes_to_cases, cases_to_judges, load_roster, and download_biographies techniques. references courtpy.politics build_table, which makes a table of each year's political context from the sources' current files, justices, which returns each justice's Martin-Quinn and Judicial Common Space scores, the tables of date ranges executives, legislatures, and high_courts, and the add_executive, add_legislature, add_high_court, load_politics, and download_politics techniques. references courtpy.courts court_table and federal_courts, the tables of courts in "instructions/{jurisdiction}/courts.csv", court_labels, which labels each case's court for tables and plots, and circuits, which finds the circuit of each case. references courtpy.scores The add_judge_scores and add_court_scores techniques, which add scores of judges and courts from training data. references courtpy.jcs medians, which loads the Judicial Common Space medians of each year, and download, which downloads the published scores with judicial-common-space, and the download_jcs technique. references courtpy.scdb cases and votes, which load the Supreme Court Database, and the add_scdb, load_scdb, and download_scdb techniques. references courtpy.fjc_idb appeals and download, which load and download the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database with fjc-idb, and the add_idb, load_idb, and download_idb techniques. core courtpy.datasets Cases, Dockets, Votes, Judges, Courts, CaseTypes, and PartyTypes, the kinds of amos.Dataset that courtpy makes, which can be saved and loaded whole. core courtpy.cases Case, and helpers for their columns (split_cell, column_as_flags, flags_as_numbers, select_whole_cases, and require_columns). core courtpy.secrets Storing and finding the CourtListener API key. core courtpy.options Defaults that a project can change before they are used.

docs.title: Saved cases
docs.text:
Both ways of collecting CourtListener cases save each case as a JSON file named for its cluster id, in a folder named for its court. Its keys are:

Key Contents source "courtlistener". court The court's id, full_name, short_name, citation_string, and jurisdiction. cluster CourtListener's opinion cluster: the case name, date filed, judges, attorneys, disposition, precedential status, and so on. docket CourtListener's whole docket (the docket number, the dates it was filed, argued, and terminated, the court appealed from, the PACER case id, the type of appeal, and so on, without the fields in options._DOCKET_SKIPPED), from the bulk data, or from the API if "dockets" was asked for. Otherwise null. citations The case's citations as text, such as "950 F.3d 12". opinions Each opinion: its type (such as "010combined" or "040dissent"), author, and one field of text (the first of options._TEXT_FIELDS that is not blank, which CourtListener recommends be "html_with_citations"). bulk_date For cases from the bulk data, the date of the files.

Lexis-Nexis cases are text files, one for each case. courtpy.lexis.split divides Lexis-Nexis downloads of many cases into such files and removes clutter such as star paging.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
courtpy.parse (or a Parser) turns each saved case into a row in three stages:

  1. A reader makes a Case with sections of text and metadata. CourtListener sections come from its data (see the table of sections in Writing Rules); a Lexis-Nexis case has one section, "text".
  2. For Lexis-Nexis, the "lexis_nexis" rules divide the text into the header and the opinions and find each part of the header.
  3. Every section except those whose names end in "_lines" is collapsed onto one line, and the rules are applied: the source's header rules (its header, such as "lexis_nexis_header", which find the court and the agencies with the jurisdiction's "courts.csv" and "agencies.csv") and "general" always, and then the rulebooks that are named ("federal" by default).

The row starts with the case's metadata, which is used instead of anything the rules find with the same name (unless the metadata is missing). A few columns are then added: author (the first of authors), panel_size, concurrences, dissents, and word_count. The text of the cases' sections (such as party, history, judges, and opinion) is not kept unless keep_text is true, because it would make the table very large.

With the text kept, the parse_all technique parses the cases again without reading the saved files, as after a change to the rules. Each case gets its source's header rules (by its source column), "general", and the rulebooks in its "rulebooks" parameter ("federal" unless it is set). A value that the rules find replaces the table's, and where they find nothing, the table's is kept. Given "rules", parse_all is amos's, which it replaces in the amos library, so settings written for amos still work.

[wrangler]
techniques = "load_court_listener, parse_all, drop_text_columns"

[load_court_listener_parameters]
keep_text = true

[parse_all_parameters]
rulebooks = "federal, deference.csv"

Parsing a large set of cases takes a while. Pass workers (the number of processes) to parse to use more of your computer.

docs.title: The case table
docs.text:
The table is labeled by "case_id": the CourtListener cluster id, or the name of the Lexis-Nexis file. Flags are booleans, counts are integers, and matches and names are lists. Columns of booleans or whole numbers that are missing for some cases (such as published or year) have the "boolean" and "Int64" types, which allow missing values.

Cases.save saves the whole dataset in a joblib file (with its label, history, and anything techniques have added), as the save_data technique of amos does, and its data as a table beside it: a CSV, parquet, or Excel file, named by the path's extension. Lists are written as text, separated by "; ", as the rules write several values. Cases.load loads either file: the joblib file as it was, or the table, labeled by "case_id" again and with the types that allow missing values. Every kind of courtpy dataset (Votes, Judges, and so on) saves and loads in the same way.

docs.title: Coders
docs.text:
The coders are amos techniques, so they can be named in the settings of any amos worker, and they record what they did in the dataset's history. code_parties, code_case_type, code_outcome, and tidy_cases are mungers (amos.Munger), which change and add columns without adding or removing rows, so the history lists the columns that each one changed and created. drop_text_columns is a cleaner (amos.Cleaner), which removes columns. They use the columns made by the federal rules.

Coder Adds code_parties Completes the parties' roles from their opposites (if one party is an appellant, the other is an appellee), and adds party1_appealing, party1_defending, and the same for party2. code_case_type type_criminal (the United States is a party and there is a sign of a criminal case), and each party's role in the case: party1_prosecution, party1_criminal_defendant, party1_civil_plaintiff, and party1_civil_defendant (and the same for party2). code_outcome outcome_reversal (from the header's disposition, or else from the decision that the opinion states, or else from the opinion's words anywhere), outcome_party1_won and outcome_party2_won, the winner by side (outcome_criminal_defendant_won, outcome_prosecution_won, outcome_civil_plaintiff_won, and outcome_civil_defendant_won), and appeal_by_defendant. Outcomes that cannot be known are missing. drop_text_columns Removes columns of text and lists (such as names and dates), which models cannot use. Its keep parameter names columns to keep. tidy_cases Gives columns of booleans and whole numbers with missing values the "boolean" and "Int64" types, which allow them. Tables that courtpy parses or loads are tidied already, so it is for tables made or changed in other ways.

To write your own, subclass amos.Munger and write munge (or subclass amos.Cleaner and write clean for a coder that removes rows or columns, amos.Merger and write match for one that adds the columns of another table, or amos.Shaper and write shape for one that changes what a row is). It is added to the library as soon as it is defined, so it can be named in settings:

import dataclasses

import amos


@dataclasses.dataclass
class CodeLongOpinion(amos.Munger):
    """Flags opinions longer than a number of words."""

    def munge(self, data, words = 5000, **kwargs):
        data["long_opinion"] = data["word_count"] > words
        return data

docs.title: Judges and panels
docs.text:
The federal rules find the names of each case's judges as the opinion writes them (panel_judges, authors, concurring, and dissenting), such as "LYNCH; HOWARD; THOMPSON". courtpy.judges matches those names to people, with a roster that fjc-biographies makes from the Federal Judicial Center's Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges:

import courtpy

roster = courtpy.judges.Roster.from_fjc()
roster.save()

from_fjc downloads three files of a few megabytes (federal judicial service, demographics, and professional careers) with fjc-biographies, into "raw" in "judges" in courtpy's data folder, unless they were downloaded before (update = True downloads them again, for the judges and changes since). The roster is fjc-biographies' table with one row for each court that a judge has served on, with the president who made the appointment and that president's party, the American Bar Association's rating, the Senate's vote, the judge's sex, race or ethnicity, and year of birth, the judge's career and flags for it, and the two columns that courtpy adds to find judges, aliases and court_num (see courtpy.judges.build_roster for the columns). save writes it as "roster.csv" in "judges" in courtpy's data folder, outside of any project, where the techniques below look for it. Their roster parameter names another.

The roster is a CSV file, so you can change it in a spreadsheet:

  • Add a judge, or another name that opinions use for a judge (as "First Middle Last" in the aliases column, with semicolons between names).
  • Add a column of your own, such as a score of each judge's ideology (or pass scores, a table with the judges' nid numbers, to from_fjc, or jcs = True for the judges' Judicial Common Space scores and martin_quinn = True for the justices' Martin-Quinn scores; see below). Every column of numbers or booleans that does not identify or date a judge's service is an attribute of the judge, which the techniques use.
  • Change how careers are coded with rules of your own (the rulebook argument). The built-in rules are fjc-biographies' judges.csv.

A name is matched by how much of a judge's name it gives, from the most to the least (see courtpy.judges.name_forms):

  1. A full name: any of the ways that fjc-biographies writes the judge's name (the roster's name_... columns, such as "Sandra Lea Lynch", "Sandra L. Lynch", and "Sandra Lynch", each with or without a suffix), or one of the judge's aliases.
  2. Initials and the last name: "S. Lynch", "S. L. Lynch", "S.L. Lynch", or "S. Lea Lynch", or the middle and last names ("Lea Lynch", for a judge who goes by a middle name).
  3. The last name alone (with any suffix), which is how opinions usually name judges.

Only judges who were serving in the case's year, or had left their court no more than two years before (options._JUDGE_GRACE), are considered, and the first of these ways that fits any of them is used. The judges it fits are then narrowed by the case's court: to a judge of that court, or else to a judge of a district court in its circuit (who may sit by designation), or else to a judge of any other court, such as a court of appeals or district court of another circuit (who may sit by designation). Rather than guess, a name that fits more than one judge at that step is not matched (which is why opinions add initials, as in "M. SMITH" and "N.R. SMITH"), and neither is a name on a case of a court that has no judges in the roster, such as a bankruptcy appellate panel.

Cases and judges are different things: a case table has a row for each case, and a roster a row for each court that each judge has served on. amos joins such tables with mergers, which add the columns of another table to the rows that they match without ever adding or losing a row, and shapers, which change what a row is. courtpy's techniques for judges are built from them:

Technique Adds add_biography A merger. Each row names one judge (in the column that its name parameter names, which is "judge" unless another is set), and gets the columns of that judge's row of the roster, with "judge_" (or another prefix) before their names: every attribute, and age, senior, designated (sitting on a court other than the judge's own), and district_judge, which depend on the case's year and court. All are numbers (1 and 0 for true and false). Its columns parameter names the columns to add, which can be any others of the roster too (such as judge, the judge's name, or president), and indicator names a column that says whether each judge was found. In Cases without a name, each case names the judges in panel_judges, and the columns are numbered by each judge's seat: judge_name1, judge_nid1, judge_party1, and so on for the first judge, judge_name2 and the rest for the second. Its lookup parameter can be a function (of a judge's name, the case's court, and its year) that takes the place of the roster. add_jcs A merger. add_biography with jcs as its only column (judge_jcs, or judge_jcs1 and so on in Cases), which needs a roster made with jcs = True. add_circuit A merger. The makeup of the active (not senior) judges of each case's circuit on the day it was decided: circuit_median_party, circuit_total_party, circuit_median_jcs, circuit_total_jcs, and circuit_judges (see Political context). code_panels A munger. panel_names (the judges who were found, as the roster names them), panel_found (how many, to compare with panel_size), judge_name1, judge_nid1, judge_name2, judge_nid2, and so on (each judge who was found, in the panel's order, with the Federal Judicial Center's name and nid), author_name, concurring_names, and dissenting_names, and the composition of the panel: panel_{attribute} is the mean of each attribute among its judges. So panel_woman is the share who are women, and panel_party is the mean party of the presidents who appointed them (from -1, all Democrats, to 1, all Republicans). panel_age, panel_senior, panel_designated, and panel_district_judge depend on the case's year and court. cases_to_votes A shaper. Replaces the table of cases with one row for each judge on each case, labeled by "vote_id" (such as "4567890-2"): the case's columns, case_id, judge, judge_nid, judge_{attribute}, colleagues_{attribute} (the mean among the other judges of the panel), judge_author, judge_concurred, judge_dissented, and for each outcome of the case, vote_{outcome}: the outcome, or its opposite if the judge dissented. So vote_reversal is whether the judge voted to reverse. Its outcomes parameter names the outcomes (by default, every column that starts with "outcome_"). Like every shaper, it takes label, task, and groups for the table that it makes, and must come before the data is split. votes_to_cases A shaper. Undoes cases_to_votes: the rows of each case become one row again, labeled by "case_id", with the case's columns as they were. judge and the columns that begin with judge_, colleagues_, or vote_ are removed, and each case keeps the other columns of its first row. A case with no judge who was found in the roster has no votes, so it does not come back. Without label, a label such as vote_reversal becomes the outcome it was made from (outcome_reversal), and the groups lose case_id. cases_to_judges A shaper. Makes Judges, a table with one row for each judge, labeled by "judge_nid": judge, cases (how many votes; count names it, or "none"), and the means of the columns of numbers and booleans, as group_rows takes them, so vote_reversal is the share of the judge's votes to reverse, judge_dissented the share of the judge's cases with a dissent by the judge, and type_criminal the share of the judge's cases that are criminal. Nothing about any one case is kept: text (such as court or the cases' names) and ids (such as case_id) are left out unless its keep parameter names them, or its how parameter names a summary for them, as in {"case_id": "list"}. Given a table of cases, it makes the votes first, with roster and outcomes. Without groups, the table has none, and without task, the task is inferred again, since a vote is now a share.

code_panels and cases_to_votes do what a wrangler of lists_to_rows, add_biography, group_rows would do: they make a row for each name that a case lists, find the judge that each name refers to, and (for code_panels) summarize the rows of each case. Use add_biography itself for a table that names one judge in each row. For example, to add what is known about the author of each opinion to a table of cases:

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, add_biography, drop_text_columns

[add_biography_parameters]
name = author
prefix = author_
indicator = author_found

The dataset's history records how many rows a merger matched, which is worth checking (and reporting) every time:

print(project.result.history[-2])
# {'technique': 'add_biography', 'source': '...roster.csv', 'rows': 5212, 'matched': 4980, 'created': ['author_party', ...]}

Each of them can be among a loader's "coders", so a vote can be the label of a study (see examples/cases_to_votes.ini and the recipes). In Python, courtpy.judges.vote_table makes the same table as cases_to_votes, and a Roster matches one name at a time:

row = roster.match("LYNCH", court_num = 1, year = 2020)
print(roster.names([row]), roster.describe(row, court_num = 1, year = 2020))

A loader passes its coders no parameters, so as coders they use the saved roster. To name another, list them as techniques of the wrangler instead (after the loader), with a section of parameters for each. add_biography takes the roster as its source, as every merger takes its other table, and finds a file that is named there as the project's clerk finds files: in the current folder, and then in the input folder. code_panels, cases_to_votes, and cases_to_judges take it as roster, whose path is relative to the folder that the study is run from.

docs.title: Political context
docs.text:
Three mergers add who held power on the day each case was decided. Each matches the case's date ("date_filed", unless date names another column) to a table of date ranges (with "start_date" and "end_date") with the merge_ranges technique of amos, so a table of your own with the same columns (such as a state's governors) can be its source. A date on which one range ends and the next begins (such as the day of an inauguration) gets the later one.

Technique Adds Table add_executive executive_name and executive_ideology (the president's party: -1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican). courtpy.politics.executives, from "instructions/federal/presidents.csv", where a president can be added. add_legislature senate_ideology and house_ideology: the median NOMINATE score of the members of each chamber of the Congress then sitting. courtpy.politics.legislatures, from "HSall_members.csv", the ideology of every member of every Congress (Voteview's "Member Ideology" data). add_high_court high_court_ideology: the Martin-Quinn score of the median justice in the Supreme Court's term then sitting (October to September). courtpy.politics.high_courts, from "justices.csv", the score of each justice in each term.

Higher scores are more conservative. The sources' current files (about 6 megabytes) are downloaded the first time, with judicial-common-space, and kept in "politics" in courtpy's data folder, where that package and fjc-biographies look for them too. courtpy.politics.download(overwrite = True) downloads them again, for the terms and votes since. The Martin-Quinn page sometimes refuses automated requests; then save "justices.csv" from it in a browser and put it in that folder.

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, add_executive, add_legislature, add_high_court, add_circuit, drop_text_columns

add_circuit adds the makeup of the whole circuit of each case on the day it was decided (for a district court, the circuit that hears its appeals, from "instructions/federal/courts.csv"; see courtpy.courts). The circuit's judges are those of its court of appeals in the roster who were active then: appointed, not yet gone, and not senior, since senior judges do not sit en banc. It adds circuit_median_party and circuit_total_party (the median and sum of the parties of the presidents who appointed them), circuit_median_jcs and circuit_total_jcs (of their Judicial Common Space scores, if the roster was made with jcs = True), and circuit_judges.

courtpy.politics.build_table still makes a table of each year's political context (president_party, supreme_court_median, supreme_court_min, supreme_court_max, senate_median, and house_median), which load_politics and download_politics load to study the years themselves, and which the merge_keys technique of amos can add to cases by "year".

courtpy.politics.justices returns the Martin-Quinn score of each justice in each term, from the same "justices.csv", with the score put on the scale of the Judicial Common Space by judicial-common-space (jcs), for studies of the Supreme Court (see below).

docs.title: The Judicial Common Space
docs.text:
The Judicial Common Space (Epstein, Martin, Segal, and Westerland, 2007) puts judges, justices, members of Congress, and presidents on one scale of ideology, on which higher scores are more conservative. A judge's score is the NOMINATE score of the judge's home-state senators of the appointing president's party, or else of the president, and a justice's is the justice's Martin-Quinn score, put on the same scale. judicial-common-space computes the scores from their sources, which courtpy uses in three ways:

Scores How courtpy adds them Each appointment of a judge or justice Roster.from_fjc(jcs = True) adds jcs to the roster, with fjc-biographies. The published scores are of the judges of the courts of appeals and the justices; the computed ones are of district judges too. Each justice in each term courtpy.politics.justices returns jcs beside martin_quinn, by term and the Supreme Court Database's numbers for the justices. Each year's medians courtpy.jcs.medians reads the published file of medians: jcs_president, jcs_house_median, jcs_senate_median, jcs_supreme_court_median, and jcs_circuit{n}_median and jcs_circuit{n}_sd for each court of appeals (numbered as court_num numbers them).

The scores of judges become an attribute of a roster, so the judge techniques use them like any other: code_panels adds panel_jcs (the mean score of each panel), and add_biography and cases_to_votes add judge_jcs (and colleagues_jcs). The files that they are computed from (Voteview's NOMINATE scores, the dates of senators' service, Wikipedia's lists of circuit judges' duty stations, and the justices' Martin-Quinn scores) are downloaded into courtpy's data folder the first time. martin_quinn = True also adds each appointment to the Supreme Court's Martin-Quinn scores (mq_first, mq_last, mq_mean, and mq_terms); pass the path of a "justices.csv" that you saved in a browser if the Martin-Quinn page refuses the download:

roster = courtpy.judges.Roster.from_fjc(jcs = True, martin_quinn = True)
roster.save()

medians has a row for each year, so it can be added to cases by "year" with the merge_keys technique of amos, or be a part of build_table (build_table(common_space = True)), whose columns already start with "jcs_". judicial-common-space downloads the published archive of scores (about 100 kilobytes) the first time it is needed, and keeps its CSV files in "jcs" in courtpy's data folder (courtpy.jcs.download(overwrite = True) downloads it again).

docs.title: The Supreme Court Database
docs.text:
The Supreme Court Database codes every case that the Supreme Court has decided since its 1946 term: the issue, the direction of the decision, what the court did with the decision below, which party won, and how each justice voted. add_scdb (a merger) adds its coding to parsed cases of the Supreme Court, with "scdb_" before the database's names for its columns:

[load_court_listener_parameters]
courts = scotus
coders = code_parties, code_case_type, code_outcome, add_scdb

A case is matched by the database's id for it, which CourtListener records for cases of the Supreme Court (the scdb_id column), or else by one of its citations (the citation column), such as "347 U.S. 483". Rather than guess, a case whose citations are those of more than one case of the database (as short orders on one page of a reporter are) is not matched. The history records how many cases were matched and the release of the database that was used.

The latest release is downloaded from the database's data page the first time, and kept in "scdb" in courtpy's data folder (courtpy.scdb.download(overwrite = True) looks for a newer one). As a technique of the wrangler, add_scdb takes a merger's parameters: source (a file of the database that you downloaded yourself), columns (such as "issueArea, decisionDirection, partyWinning"), prefix, and indicator, and on, other_on, and citations for the columns to match by. The database's online codebook explains each variable.

In Python, courtpy.scdb.cases returns the database's table with a row for each case, and courtpy.scdb.votes its table with a row for each justice in each case. The Martin-Quinn and Judicial Common Space scores of courtpy.politics.justices use the database's numbers for the justices, so a merger adds each justice's scores to each vote:

import amos
import courtpy

votes = amos.mergers.MergeKeys().apply(
    courtpy.scdb.votes(),
    source = courtpy.politics.justices(),
    on = ["term", "justice"])
print(votes.data[["caseName", "justiceName", "vote", "martin_quinn", "jcs"]].head())
print(votes.history[-1]["matched"])

docs.title: The Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database
docs.text:
The Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (IDB) has a record of each appeal in the federal courts of appeals since the 2008 fiscal year, taken from the courts' own dockets: the type of appeal, the parties, the court and judge appealed from, the dates of each step (docketed, briefed, heard, decided), the judges of the panel and the opinions each wrote, how the appeal ended, whether the decision was published, and whether a party was pro se, among much else. It covers the twelve regional circuits, not the Federal Circuit. courtpy reads it with fjc-idb, whose codebooks explain each column.

add_idb (a merger) adds the database's record of each appeal, with "idb_" before fjc-idb's names for the columns. The database has a record for each docket, and a case that consolidated several appeals has several docket numbers, so add it to Dockets (after cases_to_dockets), whose rows each have one docket number ("docket"), and each appeal gets its own record. Added to Cases, a case gets the record of the first of its docket numbers that the database has. dockets_to_cases makes the dockets cases again (with the first docket's record), and dockets_to_votes makes a row for each judge on each docket. Use them as techniques of the wrangler, after the loader:

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, cases_to_dockets, add_idb

[add_idb_parameters]
columns = appeal_type, pro_se_party, in_forma_pauperis, appeal_date, judgment_date, notice_to_judgment
indicator = in_idb

A case is matched by its circuit (the court_num column that the federal rules make, or else CourtListener's court id in court) and its docket number (docket_numbers, or else docket_number), so cases from Lexis-Nexis are matched too. "17-1234-cv", "No. 17-1234", and "17-01234" are the same docket. A case with several docket numbers (consolidated appeals) is matched by the first one that the database has. An appeal that was reopened, or remanded by the Supreme Court, has a record for each time it ended under the same docket number, so the record whose judgment is nearest the date of the decision is used, and never the record of an appeal docketed after the decision. Cases of other courts, and of years before 2008, are not matched.

Without a source, the records are those of the years of the cases: from the year of the earliest decision to the year after the latest, since the database's years are fiscal years that end on September 30. start_year and stop_year set others. The yearly files that are missing are downloaded from the Federal Judicial Center (about 10 to 20 MB a year) and kept in "fjc_idb" in courtpy's data folder, in fjc-idb's layout. Set folder to use files you already have, or download = false to download nothing. district = true also adds the district court's record of the case that was appealed (in columns that begin with "idb_district_", which fjc-idb's merge_district finds), from the district courts' files of civil cases and criminal defendants, which are about 400 MB a year.

Reading the yearly files takes a few seconds a year. To read them once, save the table and name the file as the source (a parquet file, as here, keeps the types of its columns):

import courtpy

courtpy.fjc_idb.appeals(2008, 2026).to_parquet("data/appeals.parquet")

[add_idb_parameters]
source = appeals.parquet

The CSV file that the fjc-idb command makes is a source too:

fjc-idb appellate --start-year 2008 --download --data-folder data/fjc_idb

In Python, courtpy.fjc_idb.appeals returns the database's table of appeals for a range of years, and courtpy.fjc_idb.download downloads the yearly files that are missing (with overwrite = True, the current year's file again, which the Federal Judicial Center updates during the year). fjc-idb's own functions (such as fjc_idb.run and fjc_idb.merge_district) work on the same folder.

docs.title: Comparing a study with the database
docs.text:
compare_with_idb (an explorer) asks two questions of a study of the courts of appeals. Do its variables agree with the database's? And how do the appeals it lacks differ from the ones it has? It works on Cases or Dockets. Cases are compared as dockets (see cases_to_dockets), but the dataset stays as it was, and each docket is matched to its record as add_idb matches it. It takes add_idb's parameters for finding the database (source, start_year, folder, and so on).

[explorer]
techniques = compare_with_idb

[compare_with_idb_parameters]
source = appeals.parquet
by = circuit
visualize = true

The first table, tables["compare_with_idb"], has a row for each variable that both have, among the dockets that were matched:

Variable The study's column The database's column criminal type_criminal appeal_type is a criminal appeal civil type_civil appeal_type is not a criminal appeal reversal outcome_reversal disposition is reversed (in whole or part) or remanded published published published dissent dissents (more than 0) dissents (more than 0) us_appellant a party is united_states and appellant us_appellant pro_se_appellant pro_se_appellant pro_se_appellant prisoner_appeal prisoner_appeal prisoner_appeal

A variable whose column the study lacks is left out. The table counts the dockets with both values ("compared") and those that agree ("matches", "match_share", and Cohen's "kappa", which discounts the agreement that chance would give). It also counts the disagreements in each direction: "data_only" is true in the study and false in the database, and "idb_only" is the reverse. variables picks some of them by name (such as variables = criminal, reversal). In Python, it can also add others, each as a column of the study and a column of the database:

import courtpy

cases = courtpy.parse("data/courtlistener")
dockets = courtpy.code(cases, ["cases_to_dockets"])
compare = courtpy.fjc_idb.CompareWithIdb()
table = compare.describe(
    dockets, source = "appeals.parquet",
    variables = {"en_banc": ("en_banc", "enbanc")})

The second table, tables["compare_with_idb_missing"], starts from the database, which has every appeal, so the study always lacks some. It keeps the appeals of the study's circuits that were judged between the study's first and last decisions. Unless merits_only = false, it keeps only those decided on the merits, since procedural terminations rarely have opinions. Then, for each circuit (or each district court appealed from, with by = district) and for all of them ("All"), and for each variable of report, it reports:

  • "appeals", "in_data", and "coverage": how many appeals there are, how many the study has, and the share it has.
  • "share_in_data" and "share_missing": the share that are true among the appeals the study has and among those it lacks.
  • "difference" and "p_value": the first share minus the second, and the p value of a two-proportion z test of that difference.

So a positive "difference" in reversals means the study's appeals were reversed more often than the ones it lacks, as studies of published opinions usually are.

With visualize, idb_confusion_matrices draws a confusion matrix for each variable of the first table. idb_missing_differences draws the second table as a grid of groups and variables, shaded by the difference, with a star where the p value is below alpha (0.05 unless set). The figures are in figures under the tables' names.

docs.title: Figures and checks
docs.text:
courtpy's plots, evaluators, and inferer are amos techniques for the "artist" and "critic" stages, so a settings file names them as it names amos's own. The plots need the packages of the analysis extra (pip install courtpy[analysis]); the checks need none.

Courts are labeled with their feature_name in "courts.csv" (such as "Tenth Circuit"), in the order of the table. A rate in a plot is the share of the cases that have a flag (or the mean of a number), measured from the cases themselves, so it has no confidence interval; each bar says how many cases it counts. The column of a rate is the dataset's label unless "column" is set.

Technique Draws or checks Needs court_rates The rate of a column in each court, with the rate of all the courts as a line. Cases. cases_over_time The number of cases of each court in each year, a panel for each court in the data. Cases, with year. issues_over_time The number of cases with each issue in "issues" (columns of flags, such as criminal_firearm or type_immigration) in each court in each year, a panel for each court in the data. Cases, with year. panel_composition The rate of a column for each composition of the panel by the parties of the presidents who appointed its judges ("DDD" to "RRR"), split by "by" (such as type_criminal). Cases, after add_biography or code_panels. lower_court_rates The rate of a column for each court below (lower_court_name), grouped by the court that reviewed it. Cases. trends_by_administration The yearly rate of a column in each court, with the terms of Democratic and Republican presidents shaded. Cases, with year. judge_network The judges, joined by how often they sat together (or, with "dissents", how often one dissented from the other), colored by party. Votes. audit_random_assignment Whether the traits of cases that a panel cannot change (such as type_criminal and review_agency) are balanced across panel compositions within each court and year, with a permutation test. Cases, after add_biography or code_panels. audit_parsing How many cases lack a court, a court below, judges, a year, or an outcome, have panels of another size, or have a header's disposition that disagrees with the opinion's stated decision, with examples to read. Cases. audit_coverage The cases of each court and year against the appeals that the Integrated Database records, and the share that the data has (and of published opinions). Cases, and the database (downloaded, or "source"). validate_coding How often courtpy's coding agrees with another source's ("pairs", such as published = idb_published after add_idb), with Cohen's kappa. Cases. panel_effects The effect of the colleagues' party on a judge's vote, with the judge's party and their product, a fixed effect for each court and year, standard errors clustered by case, and a randomization test that reassigns colleagues within each court and year. Votes. 
[study_project]
study_workers = "wrangler, artist, critic"

[wrangler]
techniques = "load_court_listener, add_biography"

[artist]
techniques = "court_rates, cases_over_time, issues_over_time, panel_composition"

[issues_over_time_parameters]
issues = "criminal_firearm, type_immigration"

[panel_composition_parameters]
by = "type_criminal"

[critic]
techniques = "audit_parsing, audit_random_assignment"

docs.title: Loaders
docs.text:
amos loads a project's data with loaders, the first techniques of the wrangler, so a project with a loader needs no item. courtpy's loaders are a genre of amos loaders, CaseLoader. load_court_listener and load_lexis_nexis are SourceLoaders, which download cases (if asked) and parse a folder of them; a study can add its own sources, ways to download, and loaders (see Building a Study):

Loader Source Does load_court_listener A folder of saved CourtListener cases. Defaults to "courtlistener". Downloads cases into the folder (if "download" is set), parses them, and codes them. load_lexis_nexis A folder of Lexis-Nexis cases, one per text file. Defaults to "lexis_nexis". Divides any "batches" into the folder, parses the cases, and codes them. load_cases A dataset saved by Cases.save (or courtpy parse): its joblib file or its table. Loads the dataset (a joblib file of Votes is Votes again), or the table as Cases, with its types. It applies no coders unless "coders" names some.

Their parameters go in a "{loader}_parameters" section of the settings:

Parameter Loaders Meaning source all The folder (or, for load_cases, the file) to load. coders all Techniques to apply after parsing. Defaults to "code_parties, code_case_type, code_outcome" ("none" for load_cases). Use "none" for none. save all File to save the coded table to (".csv", ".parquet", or ".xlsx"), with the whole dataset beside it in a joblib file of the same name. reuse all Whether to load the saved dataset, if there is one, instead of collecting, parsing, and coding again. label, task, groups all As in amos. They default to those in the "general" section. download load_court_listener "bulk" to extract cases from the bulk data, "api" to download them with the API, a way that a study adds, or "none" (the default) to use the cases already in the folder. Any parameter that the loader does not know is an option of the way to download. courts load_court_listener CourtListener court ids (such as "ca1, ca2") or groups (federal_appellate, federal_circuits, or scotus). start_date, end_date load_court_listener Dates filed (YYYY-MM-DD). max_cases, overwrite load_court_listener Most cases to download, and whether to download cases saved before. dockets load_court_listener For "api", whether to download each case's docket too (one more request per case). bulk_folder, bulk_date, stream load_court_listener For "bulk", where to keep the bulk files, which date's files to use, and whether to read them from CourtListener without saving them. batches load_lexis_nexis Files (or folders) of many cases to divide into the source folder first. rulebooks load_court_listener, load_lexis_nexis Rules to parse with: built-in names ("federal", or any of "citations", "civil", "constitutional", "criminal", and "agencies") or CSV files or folders. The source's header rules and "general" are always applied. Defaults to "federal". keep_text, limit, workers load_court_listener, load_lexis_nexis Whether to keep the opinions' text, most cases to parse, and processes to parse with.

The loaders work through the project's clerk, as amos loaders do. A folder or file named by a relative path is looked for in the current folder and then in the clerk's input folder (the "input_folder" of the "files" section), where downloads save their cases, and "save" is in the clerk's interim folder ("interim_folder"). The label is checked after the coders run, so it can be a column that a coder makes (such as outcome_reversal), and the dataset's history records the loader and then each coder.

A loader can also be used without a project. apply takes the dataset so far, or None to start a new one, and returns an amos.Dataset:

dataset = courtpy.loaders.LoadCourtListener().apply(
    None, source = "courtlistener", label = "outcome_reversal")

docs.title: Reference tables
docs.text:
Some studies are not of cases: of how the justices vote, of the appeals in the Integrated Database, or of the judges themselves. Reference loaders (a genre of amos loaders, ReferenceLoader) start such a study with a table of reference data. Each "load_" technique loads the files that courtpy keeps outside of projects (or a file named as its source), downloading them first if they are missing, and each "download_" technique downloads them into the folder named as its source (or courtpy's own), again if refresh is true, and then loads them. Without a source, the history records it as "current".

Loader Table Other parameters load_roster A saved roster of judges (see courtpy.judges.Roster). download_biographies A roster made from the Federal Judicial Center's files. refresh, jcs, martin_quinn, scores, rulebook, and save (true, or a path, to save the roster). load_scdb, download_scdb The Supreme Court Database's cases or, with kind = votes, each justice's vote in each case. kind, and refresh and session to download. load_idb, download_idb The Integrated Database's appeals. start_year, stop_year, district, fix_city_spellings, and download (to load) or refresh (to download). load_politics, download_politics The political context of each year (see courtpy.politics.build_table), or a saved table of years. supreme_court, congress, score, and common_space, and refresh and session to download. download_jcs The Judicial Common Space medians of each year or, with kind, the scores of each judge or justice. kind, refresh, and session. 
[wrangler]
techniques = load_scdb

[load_scdb_parameters]
kind = votes
label = majority

To add a reference table's columns to cases instead, use its merger (add_biography, add_scdb, add_idb, or add_executive).

docs.title: The CourtListener API
docs.text:
A free CourtListener account can make 5 requests a minute, 50 an hour, and 125 a day (as of 2026); members have more. CourtListener asks for 20 cases (one page of opinion clusters) in one request and their opinions in one more, so a free account can download roughly a thousand cases a day.

  • Requests are at least min_interval seconds apart (1 by default).
  • When CourtListener asks for a pause (an HTTP 429 response), the client waits as long as it is asked, up to max_wait seconds (an hour by default), which rides out the minute and hour limits. A longer pause (the daily limit) raises a RateLimitError.
  • The place in each court's list of cases is saved in a ".courtpy" folder inside the download folder, so running the same download again resumes it. Running a finished download again takes one request for each court and saves any cases added since.
  • download_case downloads one case by its cluster id.

docs.title: The bulk data
docs.text:
CourtListener publishes its whole database every three months, at https://com-courtlistener-storage.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/list.html?prefix=bulk-data/. BulkData.extract reads five files, in this order: courts, dockets (about 5 GB), opinion clusters (about 2.5 GB), citations, and opinions (about 55 GB). It keeps only the cases of the courts and dates asked for, so it needs little memory, but reading the opinions file takes hours. The dockets file is read a second time after the opinion clusters, to save each case with its whole docket. Extract every court and year you may need at once.

The files are read with amos's read_chunks, which decompresses and parses them on every core and drops the rows of other courts and cases before they become Python objects. BulkData.chunks yields those chunks as tables, with the columns and values to keep, for studies that need other parts of the bulk data.

By default, the files are downloaded (resuming an interrupted download) and kept in "bulk" in courtpy's data folder, outside of any project, so they can be used again. Set folder to keep them elsewhere, date to use older files (available() lists the dates), or stream = True to read them from CourtListener without saving them.

docs.title: Keeping your API key secret
docs.text:
Your API key, if you use one, is never written in a project's files or in courtpy itself. Store it once:

courtpy key set

That asks for the key (without showing it) and stores it in your computer's keyring (Windows Credential Manager, the macOS Keychain, or the Secret Service on Linux), or, if there is none, in a private file in your user folder (the secrets file, at courtpy.secrets.secrets_path()). From then on, courtpy finds it whenever it is needed. courtpy key show says where it was found (with most of it hidden), and courtpy key delete removes it.

courtpy looks for the key in this order: the COURTLISTENER_API_KEY environment variable, the keyring, the secrets file, and a .env file in the current folder (with a line such as COURTLISTENER_API_KEY=your-key; keep such a file out of version control). In Python, use courtpy.secrets.set_api_key(...) and courtpy.secrets.get_api_key(). set_api_key stores the key in the keyring if there is one and in the secrets file otherwise (or where its store argument says).

docs.title: Folders
docs.text: Folder Holds Default Changed with Configuration The secrets file. "courtpy" in %APPDATA% (Windows) or ~/.config COURTPY_CONFIG_DIR Data Bulk data files, the roster of judges and the files it is made from, and the files of Martin-Quinn scores, NOMINATE scores, Judicial Common Space scores, and the Supreme Court Database. "courts" in the data folder of the amos workspace (courtpy.options._DATA_SUBFOLDER), where every amos project keeps its data: with projects in "projects/code", it is "projects/data/courts". The workspace is the folder named by AMOS_WORKSPACE, or else the folder that holds the nearest "code" folder above the current folder COURTPY_DATA_DIR

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
courtpy.options holds defaults as module-level constants, which a project can change before they are used. For example, to wait at least two seconds between requests to the API, or to add a group of courts:

import courtpy

courtpy.options._MIN_INTERVAL = 2.0
courtpy.options._COURT_GROUPS["new_england"] = ("ca1", "mad", "nhd", "med", "rid")

docs.title: Errors you may see
docs.text: Error Cause MissingAPIKeyError: no CourtListener API key was found The API needs a key. Run courtpy key set, or use the bulk data. CourtListenerError: CourtListener rejected the request (401) The key is wrong. Check it with courtpy key show. RateLimitError: CourtListener asked courtpy to wait ... hours The account's daily limit was reached. Run the same download again later. ValueError: ... row N: the pattern ... is not valid A rule's regular expression has an error. courtpy rules file.csv checks a file. KeyError: 'code_outcome' needs the columns [...] A coder needs columns made by the federal rules. ValueError: no courtlistener cases were found in ... The loader's source folder has no saved cases. Set "download" or "source". ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'statsmodels' logit_sm (and the other statsmodels models) need statsmodels. Use logit for scikit-learn's logistic regression, or pip install amos[statistics]. KeyError: the label 'outcome_reversal' is not a column of the data The label is made by a coder that was not run. Check the "coders" setting. FileNotFoundError: there is no roster of judges at ... add_biography, code_panels, and cases_to_votes need a roster. Make and save one with courtpy.judges.Roster.from_fjc().save(), or name one with the "source" parameter of add_biography or the "roster" parameter of the others. KeyError: 'add_executive' needs the columns ['date_filed'] add_executive, add_legislature, add_high_court, and add_circuit match each case's date. Set their "date" to the column that has it. TypeError: 'merge_keys' cannot match 'year', which is text in the data, with 'year', which is numbers in the other table The cases' years are not numbers (as they are in a table that was saved and loaded without courtpy.Cases.load). Load the table with Cases.load (or load_cases), or change the column with a cleaner such as clean_numbers. KeyError: 'add_scdb' needs the column 'scdb_id' ... or 'citation' add_scdb matches cases by the Supreme Court Database's ids, which CourtListener records for cases of the Supreme Court, or by their citations. Set its "on" or "citations" to the columns that have them. ValueError: '...' changes the rows of the data, so it must come before the data is split cases_to_votes is a shaper, which came after a splitter. Put it in the wrangler (or among a loader's coders). ImportError: cannot import 'fairlearn.metrics...' A study has "groups" (such as case_id, for judges' votes), so the scorecard compares the model across them, which needs fairlearn. Name the scorecard's "metrics", or pip install amos[fairness].
