docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Short answers to common jobs. See the tutorial for the basics and the advanced user guide for every setting.

docs.title: Study only criminal appeals
docs.text:
outcome_criminal_defendant_won is missing for civil cases, so keep only the criminal cases (and those whose winner is known) before using it as a label. This study loads a table of cases saved earlier (with courtpy parse or Cases.save):

[general]
seed = 43
label = outcome_criminal_defendant_won

[criminal_project]
criminal_workers = wrangler, analyst, critic

[wrangler]
techniques = load_cases, filter_rows, drop_missing, drop_text_columns

[load_cases_parameters]
source = cases.csv

[filter_rows_parameters]
query = type_criminal

[drop_missing_parameters]
columns = outcome_criminal_defendant_won

[analyst]
techniques = stratified, logit

[critic]
techniques = scorecard

Columns that record the outcome itself (such as outcome_reversal, disposition_reverse, and opinion_reverse) would give the answer away, so drop them (with drop_columns) or name the features to keep (with keep_columns), as in the example study.

docs.title: Study how judges vote
docs.text:
To study judges rather than cases, first make a roster of judges, once (see Judges and panels):

import courtpy

courtpy.judges.Roster.from_fjc().save()

Then add code_panels and cases_to_votes to the loader's coders. cases_to_votes is a shaper, which changes what a row is: the table has one row for each judge on each case, and vote_reversal (whether the judge voted to reverse) can be the label. This is the heart of examples/cases_to_votes.ini:

[general]
seed = 43
label = vote_reversal
groups = case_id

[votes_project]
votes_workers = wrangler, analyst, critic

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, filter_rows, keep_columns, drop_missing

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = courtlistener
coders = code_parties, code_case_type, code_outcome, code_panels, add_executive, cases_to_votes

[filter_rows_parameters]
query = type_criminal and panel_size == 3 and panel_found == 3

[keep_columns_parameters]
columns = court_num, year, executive_ideology, judge_party, judge_woman, judge_age, colleagues_party, colleagues_woman

[analyst]
techniques = group_split, logit

[critic]
techniques = scorecard

[scorecard_parameters]
metrics = roc_auc, accuracy, balanced_accuracy, f1
  • The query keeps criminal appeals decided by three judges (so not by a court sitting en banc) who were all found in the roster. Compare panel_found with panel_size to see how many panels have a judge who was not found.
  • The judges of a case decide it together, so groups = case_id and group_split keep them together when the data is split, and a model is tested on cases that it has not seen.
  • A scorecard compares a model across a study's groups unless its metrics are named. Here the groups are cases, so that comparison would mean nothing (and it needs the optional fairlearn package).

To study panels instead, use code_panels without cases_to_votes. The table keeps one row for each case, the label can stay outcome_reversal, and the composition of each panel (such as panel_party and panel_woman) can be among the features. votes_to_cases turns a table of votes back into a table of cases, so columns added to the votes can be studied by case.

To study the judges themselves, add cases_to_judges after cases_to_votes (or in its place, with the roster as its roster). It makes one row for each judge, with how many cases the judge decided (cases), the judge's attributes, and the shares of the judge's votes, such as vote_reversal (the share to reverse) and judge_dissented (the share of the judge's cases with a dissent by the judge):

[general]
seed = 43
label = judge_dissented

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = courtlistener
coders = code_parties, code_case_type, code_outcome, cases_to_votes, cases_to_judges

docs.title: Add what is known about each opinion's author
docs.text:
add_biography is a merger: it adds the columns of the roster's row for the judge that each row names, and never adds or loses a row. To study whether the author of an opinion matters, name the column with the author's name and a prefix for the new columns:

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, add_biography, filter_rows, keep_columns

[add_biography_parameters]
name = author
prefix = author_
indicator = author_found

[filter_rows_parameters]
query = type_criminal and author_found

[keep_columns_parameters]
columns = outcome_reversal, court_num, year, author_party, author_woman, author_age, author_prosecutor

The history of the study's result records how many cases' authors were found (its "matched"), which belongs in a description of the data.

docs.title: Add the politics of the day
docs.text:
add_executive adds the president on the day each case was decided and the president's party, add_legislature the median NOMINATE score of each chamber of the Congress then sitting, add_high_court the Martin-Quinn score of the Supreme Court's median justice in the term then sitting, and add_circuit the makeup of the whole circuit's active judges (courtpy downloads the scores from their sources the first time):

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, add_executive, add_legislature, add_high_court, add_circuit, drop_text_columns

Each matches the case's date ("date_filed") to a table of date ranges, so a table of your own with the same columns (such as a state's governors) can be its source. See Political context.

docs.title: Score judges and courts from training data
docs.text:
cases_to_judges and cases_to_courts summarize the cases of a training set, one row for each judge or court. Save the table, and add_judge_scores and add_court_scores add its columns to the cases of a test set, matched by the judge's or court's number:

import courtpy

training = courtpy.Cases.load("training.csv")
judges = courtpy.code(training, "cases_to_judges")
judges.save("judge_scores.csv")

[wrangler]
techniques = load_cases, code_panels, add_judge_scores

[add_judge_scores_parameters]
source = judge_scores.csv
columns = vote_reversal, judge_dissented

In Cases, each judge's scores are numbered by the judge's seat (judge_score_vote_reversal1, ...), and code_panels (or add_biography) must come first, to find each seat's judge.

docs.title: Use the Supreme Court Database's coding
docs.text:
For cases of the Supreme Court, add_scdb adds the Supreme Court Database's coding of each case, with "scdb_" before the database's names for its variables. courtpy downloads the latest release the first time:

[general]
label = outcome_reversal

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, add_scdb, filter_rows, keep_columns

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = courtlistener
download = bulk
courts = scotus
start_date = 2000-01-01

[add_scdb_parameters]
columns = issueArea, decisionDirection, lcDispositionDirection
indicator = in_scdb

[filter_rows_parameters]
query = in_scdb

[keep_columns_parameters]
columns = outcome_reversal, year, scdb_issueArea, scdb_lcDispositionDirection

See The Supreme Court Database.

docs.title: Add the Federal Judicial Center's record of each appeal
docs.text:
For cases of the courts of appeals, add_idb adds the record of each appeal in the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database, which comes from the courts' dockets: what an opinion does not say, such as whether a party was pro se and how long the appeal took. The database has a record for each docket, so cases_to_dockets first makes a row for each docket number of each case (a case that consolidated several appeals has several). courtpy downloads the years of the cases the first time:

[general]
label = outcome_reversal
; The dockets of a case are kept together when the data is split.
groups = case_id

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, cases_to_dockets, add_idb, filter_rows, keep_columns, drop_missing

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = courtlistener
download = bulk
courts = federal_circuits
start_date = 2015-01-01
end_date = 2019-12-31

[add_idb_parameters]
columns = pro_se_party, notice_to_judgment, criminal_direct_appeal, civil_us_party
indicator = in_idb

[filter_rows_parameters]
query = in_idb

[keep_columns_parameters]
columns = outcome_reversal, year, court_num, idb_pro_se_party, idb_notice_to_judgment, idb_criminal_direct_appeal, idb_civil_us_party

idb_notice_to_judgment is the number of days from the notice of appeal to the judgment. See The Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database for how cases are matched and how to use files you already have.

docs.title: Add your own variables
docs.text:
Write the rules in a CSV file (see Writing Rules) and parse with the federal rules and yours:

column,name,kind,pattern,value,flags,separator,note
opinion,cites_chevron,flags,Chevron(?: U\.S\.A\.)?(?:,)? Inc\. v\. Natural Res,,ignorecase,,Chevron deference
opinion,cites_loper_bright,flags,Loper Bright,,ignorecase,,
opinion,chevron_mentions,counts,\bChevron\b,,,,

table = courtpy.parse("courtlistener", rulebooks = ["federal", "deference.csv"])

or, in a settings file, rulebooks = federal, deference.csv in the loader's parameters (such as the "load_court_listener_parameters" section). Check the file first with courtpy rules deference.csv.

For a quick look without a file of rules, keep the opinions' text and search it with amos's parsers, such as parse_flags and parse_counts, after the loader. drop_text_columns then removes the text before the analysis:

[wrangler]
techniques = "load_court_listener, parse_flags, parse_counts, drop_text_columns"

[load_court_listener_parameters]
keep_text = true

[parse_flags_parameters]
column = "opinion"
name = "cites_loper_bright"
pattern = 'Loper Bright'
flags = "ignorecase"

[parse_counts_parameters]
column = "opinion"
name = "chevron_mentions"
pattern = '\bChevron\b'

courtpy's rulebooks are techniques too (parse_federal, parse_civil, parse_criminal, and so on), which search a dataset's sections of text in the same way.

docs.title: Turn names and citations into lists or columns
docs.text:
The judges, citations, and docket numbers of a case are text, with "; " between them (such as "LYNCH; HOWARD; THOMPSON"). The split_values coder turns them into lists, or into a column for each (panel_judges_1, panel_judges_2, and so on):

listed = courtpy.code(table, ["split_values"]).data
wide = courtpy.code(
    table, ["split_values"],
    parameters = {"split_values": {"columns": "panel_judges", "into": "columns"}}).data

To make a row for each judge instead, use amos's lists_to_rows with separator = ";".

docs.title: Keep a set of recent cases up to date
docs.text:
A download with the API saves its place, and running it again saves only the cases added since. Run the same command each week (for example, with Windows Task Scheduler or cron):

courtpy download api --courts federal_circuits --start 2026-01-01 --folder courtlistener

docs.title: Parse cases downloaded from Lexis-Nexis
docs.text:
courtpy split downloads --folder lexis_nexis
courtpy parse lexis_nexis --source lexis_nexis --output lexis_cases.csv

The second command also codes the parties, case types, and outcomes (add --no-code to skip that).

docs.title: Look at what the rules found in one case
docs.text:
import courtpy

case = courtpy.courtlistener.read_case("courtlistener/ca1/4567890.json")
print(case.sections["judges"])
parser = courtpy.Parser.create("federal", keep_text = True)
row = parser.parse(case)
print(row["panel_judges"], row["disposition"], row["disposition_reverse"])

docs.title: Use the table in Stata or R
docs.text: The CSV file that Cases.save writes can be read by Stata (import delimited cases.csv), R (read.csv("cases.csv")), and most other programs. Lists (such as the judges) are written as text, with "; " between the items.

docs.title: Instructions: the rules that parse court opinions
docs.text:
courtpy finds information in court opinions with rules written in CSV files, which can be opened and changed in Excel, Google Sheets, or any spreadsheet. Each row is one rule. You can change these files, or make your own and pass them to courtpy (rulebooks = my_rules.csv in a settings file, or courtpy.parse(folder, rulebooks = ["federal", "my_rules.csv"]) in Python).

The rules are in three folders:

  • general has the rules that fit opinions of any jurisdiction.
  • federal has the rules that fit only federal opinions. A file here adds to the general file of the same name and does not repeat its rules. A topic with no federal rules (such as citations) has no file here.
  • sources has a folder for each source of cases (courtlistener and lexis_nexis) with the rules that fit only its cases: header.csv, and for Lexis-Nexis, the rules that divide a case into its parts, with a file for each kind of court (federal_appellate.csv, for the federal courts of appeals).

Some files of federal are tables that rules are made from, or that courtpy reads, rather than rules:

  • courts.csv has a row for each federal court: courtpy's number for it, its name, its name as a label for tables and plots (feature_name), its level (high, appellate, trial, or specialty), its circuit, CourtListener's id for it (courtlistener_name), and patterns of the names that the Federal Judicial Center and opinions use for it (see courtpy.courts). The header rules find each case's court with it (by CourtListener's id, or by the names in a Lexis-Nexis header) and the court whose decision is reviewed (by the names in the history), so a court added to it is found without changing the rules, and add_circuit finds each case's circuit with it.
  • agencies.csv is a topic of rules of its own (below), and the header rules are made from it too, to find the agencies named in each party and the history. In a party, an agency's name must end the party or come before a comma, semicolon, closing parenthesis, or "et al.", so that a company named for an agency (such as "FMC WYOMING CORPORATION") is not taken for it.
  • presidents.csv has the term of each president, with the president's party (-1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican). add_executive and courtpy.politics.presidents read it, so a new president can be added to it.
Topic Files What it does lexis_nexis sources/lexis_nexis/federal_appellate.csv Divides a Lexis-Nexis case into its header and opinions, and finds each part of the header (the parties, court, docket number, dates, history, counsel, disposition, citation, judges, and author). CourtListener cases do not need it, because CourtListener stores those parts separately. courtlistener_header, lexis_nexis_header general/header.csv, federal/agencies.csv, sources/courtlistener/header.csv or sources/lexis_nexis/header.csv, federal/courts.csv Finds variables in the parts of the header: each party's role, the agencies named in each party and the history (party1_agencies, party2_agencies, and history_agencies), the disposition, the counsel, citations, docket numbers, and the names of the judges (general/header.csv). Every source's rules find the trial or specialized court whose decision is reviewed in the history (lower_court_num and lower_court_name, from the courts' names in courts.csv). The Lexis-Nexis rules also find the court's number and name (court_num and court_name, from the court's names in courts.csv), the subsequent history, the Lexis citation, and the notice of an unpublished opinion; CourtListener cases have their court's number and name, and the court below's, from CourtListener's ids for them. When a CourtListener case has no roles in its header (as recent ones often do not), its rules read them from the caption at the start of the opinion. Each source's header rules are applied to its cases (header, with only the general rules and agencies, to a source with none of its own). Always applied. general general/general.csv Finds the decision that the opinion states ("AFFIRMED." or "we reverse"), its words about dispositions anywhere, procedure (such as pro se, mandamus, and mootness), and standards of review. Always applied. citations general/citations.csv Finds citations to cases, statutes, regulations, the Constitution, legislative materials, and other sources (citations_...). civil general/civil.csv, federal/civil.csv Finds the civil issues discussed: general civil issues (civil_...), torts (tort_...), contracts (contract_...), intellectual property (ip_...), and writs (writ_...). Each prefix is a case type (see code_case_type), so a new prefix (such as immigration_) is a case type too. constitutional general/constitutional.csv Finds the constitutional issues discussed (constitutional_...). criminal general/criminal.csv, federal/criminal.csv Finds the criminal issues discussed (criminal_...). review federal/review.csv Finds what kind of review an appeal is: from a federal district court (review_district), of an agency (review_agency), or of the Board of Immigration Appeals or an immigration judge (review_immigration). For an appeal from a district court, it finds the district judge as the opening names them (district_text) and their name (district_judges). agencies federal/agencies.csv Finds every federal agency that the caption, the history, or the opinion names (agencies), by its name or a common abbreviation, as the agencies' names separated by "; " (such as "Internal Revenue Service; United States Tax Court"). The agencies are those of the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database (as fjc-idb lists them), and each rule's note gives fjc-idb's code.

Each topic's rules are its general file and then its federal file, in that order. The source's header rules and general are applied to every case, whether or not they are named. The others can be chosen by name: rulebooks = civil, criminal in a settings file (or courtpy.parse(folder, rulebooks = ["civil", "criminal"]) in Python) parses with the header rules, general, civil, and criminal. The "federal" rulebook (the default) is every topic from general on, in the order above. A file named more than once is applied once.

docs.title: The columns
docs.text:
The files use the layout of amos's parse_all rulebooks, which courtpy uses to apply them. (Files in courtpy's older layout, with target, variable, ignorecase, and dotall columns and the kinds flag, count, label, labels, section, excerpts, and remove, still work: amos reads them as the rules they stand for.)

Column Meaning column The section of text to search, such as opinion, party1, or disposition. List several, separated by commas, to search each of them. name The name of the column that the rule makes. Rules with the same name are combined. A split rule names two or more. kind What the rule does (see below). pattern A regular expression to search for. Plain words work too. value For a category or categories rule, the value to record. Otherwise leave it blank. flags Any of ignorecase (to ignore the difference between capital and lower-case letters), dotall (for . in the pattern to also match line breaks), multiline, and verbose, separated by commas. Optional. separator What goes between several values in one cell, for categories, matches, and names rules. Optional: a comma and a space if blank. Every courtpy rule that makes several values uses "; ", since names and agencies can have commas in them. note Anything you want to say about the rule. courtpy ignores it.

docs.title: The kinds of rules
Things to know
docs.text:
• Rules run from top to bottom. A rule can search a section made by a rule above it (for example, party1 and party2 exist only after the split rule that makes them). Each rule searches every case at once.
  • Text is put on one line first. Before the federal rules run, every section except those whose names end in _lines has its line breaks and extra spaces replaced with single spaces, so that a phrase broken across two lines is still found. (The lexis_nexis rules run before this, so they can use line breaks, written \n.) The header rules run next, and then the federal rules.
  • Names are cleaned. A names rule makes the text upper-case and removes periods and apostrophes before splitting it, so write its pattern in capital letters.
  • Several values are text. The names, matches, and categories of a case are one cell of text, with "; " between them, such as "LYNCH; HOWARD; THOMPSON". The split_values technique turns them into lists or into a column for each value, and amos's lists_to_rows into a row for each value.
  • Rules that start with letters are fast. Python finds a pattern that begins with letters by searching for them, which is many times faster than trying the pattern at every character. A pattern that begins with \b, a group, or a class, or that ignores case (the ignorecase flag), loses that. So agencies.csv matches with case, writing a name in its capitalized form and in capitals (Federal\s+Trade\s+Commission|FEDERAL\s+TRADE\s+COMMISSION), and puts the check that an abbreviation is a whole word after its letters (NLRB\b(?<![\w-]NLRB) rather than \bNLRB\b). The check also skips an abbreviation right after a hyphen, which is usually a judge's initials at the end of a docket number (such as "06-CR-126-CAB").
  • Curly quotes and dashes are UTF-8. Some patterns have characters such as ’ (in ['’], an apostrophe of either kind) or – and —. If they show as â€™ or 'â], the spreadsheet opened the file in another encoding: open it again as UTF-8 (in LibreOffice, choose "Unicode (UTF-8)" as the character set when it asks).
  • Missing sections are not errors. If a case has no section that a rule searches (such as future in a CourtListener case), a flag is FALSE, a count is 0, and the other kinds are blank.
  • A match rule does not replace a section made by a rule above it. So two match rules for one name are a first choice and a fallback: the header rules make panel_text from the opinion's "Before ..." line, and only otherwise from the header's judges.
  • Three sets of variables record the disposition. disposition_... come from the header's disposition, decision_... from the decision that the opinion states ("AFFIRMED.", "VACATED AND REMANDED.", or "we reverse"), and opinion_... from those words anywhere in the opinion, which may be about an earlier decision or a standard of review ("we will reverse only if"). The code_outcome coder uses the first of the three that a case has.
  • Check your rules with courtpy rules my_rules.csv in a terminal. It reports any row that is not a valid rule, by its row number, and lists the columns the rules make.
  • Save files as CSV in UTF-8 ("CSV UTF-8" in Excel), so that symbols such as § are kept.

docs.title: Sections of text
docs.text:
These sections can be targets in the federal rules (and your own):

Section Lexis-Nexis CourtListener party The caption. The full case name. party1, party2 Made by the split rule in general/header.csv. The same. court The court's line in the header, which courts.csv numbers. The court's full name. (court_num comes from CourtListener's id for the court.) docket_number The docket line. The docket number (if dockets were downloaded). citation The citation line. The case's citations. dates Every line with a date, with "; " between them. (Dates come from CourtListener's data.) history "PRIOR HISTORY". The procedural history and the court appealed from. future "SUBSEQUENT HISTORY". (None.) notice "NOTICE". (None: publication comes from CourtListener's precedential status.) counsel "COUNSEL". The attorneys. disposition "DISPOSITION". The disposition (often blank). judges "JUDGES". The judges. opinion_by "OPINION BY". The authors of the majority (or lead) opinions. concurring_lines, dissenting_lines Lines about concurrences and dissents, with "; " between them. The authors of concurrences and dissents. posture, syllabus (None.) CourtListener's posture and syllabus. opinion Everything after the line "OPINION". The text of every opinion, the majority first.

The header rules make these sections from the opinion, which your own rules can search too:

Section Holds opening_lines The first 4,000 characters of the opinion (not kept in the table). caption CourtListener only: the header's caption, if it names an appellant or appellee. Otherwise, the caption in the opinion's opening, from the first party's role through the second's (such as "Plaintiff-Appellee, v. JOHN DOE, Defendant-Appellant"). caption1, caption2 CourtListener only: the caption before and after "v.", in the order of party1 and party2. panel_text The panel as the opinion's opening names it ("Before SMITH, JONES, and BROWN, Circuit Judges"). Otherwise, the judges section. decision The decision as the opinion states it.

docs.title: Rules of your own
docs.text: A file of your own can be named by its path wherever a rulebook can be named. To name it like a built-in rulebook instead (rulebooks = federal, review), make each file in a folder a rulebook with courtpy.rules.register_rulebooks(folder) when your study's package is imported. Each file is a rulebook named for its stem, and each rulebook is also a technique (such as parse_review). With several folders, each topic applies the file of the same name in each folder, in order, as courtpy applies its general and then its federal files. See Building a Study.

docs.title: Building a Study
docs.text: A study built on courtpy is a small Python package with its own settings, rules, and techniques. courtpy collects, parses, and codes the cases, and amos runs the study's workflow. This guide shows the parts a study usually has and where each one plugs into courtpy.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
my_study/
  pyproject.toml          # depends on courtpy; names the program
  studies/
    my_study.toml         # the settings of the workflow
  src/my_study/
    __init__.py           # registers the rules and techniques
    __main__.py           # the command line program
    instructions/
      careers.csv         # rules for the judges' careers (optional)
      review.csv          # the study's own rules for opinions
    measures.py           # the study's own techniques
    sources.py            # its own sources or ways to download (optional)
  tests/

docs.title: Rules of your own
docs.text:
Put the study's rules in CSV files in the layout that the rules guide describes, one file per topic. Then make each file a rulebook when the package is imported, in __init__.py:

import pathlib

import courtpy

INSTRUCTIONS = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / 'instructions'
RULEBOOKS = courtpy.rules.register_rulebooks(INSTRUCTIONS)

Each file is now a rulebook named for its stem (such as "review"), which the settings can name with courtpy's own:

[load_court_listener_parameters]
rulebooks = "federal, review"

Each one is also a technique (such as parse_review) that searches the columns of text that a loader keeps with keep_text = true.

register_rulebooks takes more than one folder. Each topic applies the file of the same name in each folder, in order, which is how courtpy applies its general rules and then its federal rules. A prefix keeps the rulebooks of two jurisdictions apart (such as "texas_civil"), and combined makes one rulebook that applies them all:

courtpy.rules.register_rulebooks(
    INSTRUCTIONS / 'general', INSTRUCTIONS / 'texas',
    prefix = 'texas', combined = 'texas')

Check a rulebook from the terminal before using it:

courtpy rules review

docs.title: Techniques of your own
docs.text:
A study's techniques are amos techniques: subclasses of an amos genre (such as amos.Munger or amos.Shaper) with a munge, shape, or apply method. Defining the class adds it to the library, so the settings can name it as soon as the package is imported. See the catalog for courtpy's techniques, which a study's settings can name in the same way.

courtpy's case tables keep several values in one cell as text with "; " between them (such as "LYNCH; HOWARD; THOMPSON"), so they can be saved as CSV files. courtpy.cases has the helpers that study code usually needs for them:

Helper Does split_cell Returns the values of a cell as a list (a list stays a list, and a missing value is an empty list). column_as_flags Returns a column as plain booleans, with missing values (or a missing column) as false, and "TRUE" or "yes" from a CSV file as true. flags_as_numbers Returns a column of flags as 1.0, 0.0, and NaN, for means and models. select_whole_cases Returns which rows a query selects, keeping all the rows of a case (such as each judge's vote) or none of them. require_columns Raises a KeyError that names the missing columns, with a hint of how to make them.

docs.title: Sources of your own
docs.text:
courtpy reads saved cases with a source (courtpy.Source) and collects them with a way to download (courtpy.Download). Like techniques, both add themselves to courtpy when they are defined, so a study can add its own in a module that its __init__.py imports.

A way to download saves cases in a folder. Its download method takes the folder, the courts (with groups already expanded), the dates, "max_cases", and "overwrite", and any options of its own, which come from the loader's parameters (as text, from a settings file) or from its command line options:

import argparse
import dataclasses
import pathlib
from typing import Any, ClassVar

import courtpy

from .bulk import OpinionData  # the study's own subclass of courtpy.BulkData


@dataclasses.dataclass
class OpinionsDownload(courtpy.Download):
    """Extracts cases from the bulk files that hold opinions."""

    name: ClassVar[str] = 'opinions'

    @classmethod
    def add_arguments(cls, parser: argparse.ArgumentParser) -> None:
        parser.add_argument('--parties', help = 'a pattern of case names')

    def download(
        self,
        folder: pathlib.Path,
        *,
        courts: list[str] | None = None,
        start_date: str | None = None,
        end_date: str | None = None,
        max_cases: int | None = None,
        overwrite: bool = False,
        parties: Any = None,
        bulk_folder: Any = None,
        **options: Any) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
        data = OpinionData(
            folder = self.locate(bulk_folder) if bulk_folder else None)
        return data.extract(
            courts or ['ca1', 'ca2'], start_date, end_date, folder,
            max_cases = max_cases, overwrite = overwrite, parties = parties)

Now load_court_listener takes download = "opinions" (and parties), and my-study download opinions --parties "United States" runs it. locate finds a folder named in the settings as the loader finds its source. A name that courtpy already uses (such as "bulk") replaces courtpy's way.

A new kind of saved case needs a source, which reads one file into a courtpy.Case, and a loader, which needs only the source's name:

@dataclasses.dataclass
class TexasCourt(courtpy.Source):
    """Reads the opinions of Texas courts, saved as text files."""

    pattern: ClassVar[str] = '*.txt'

    def read(self, path: pathlib.Path) -> courtpy.Case:
        return courtpy.Case(
            id = path.stem, source = self.name,
            sections = {'opinion': path.read_text(encoding = 'utf-8')},
            metadata = {'source': self.name}, path = path)


@dataclasses.dataclass
class LoadTexasCourt(courtpy.SourceLoader):
    """Collects, parses, and codes the opinions of Texas courts."""

    reads: ClassVar[str] = 'texas_court'
    default_source: ClassVar[str | None] = 'texas_court'

The source is named "texas_court" (the snake case name of its class, unless it sets name), and the loader is the technique load_texas_court, which takes the parameters of load_court_listener. A way to download for it sets source = 'texas_court'. A source can also set structure (a rulebook that finds the sections of each case, as Lexis-Nexis needs) and finish (which adds columns to each parsed case). The catalog lists the sources and ways to download that courtpy has.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The settings describe the workflow, as in any amos project. A study of votes on the courts of appeals might be:

[general]
seed = 43

[files]
input_folder = "data"
interim_folder = "data"
output_folder = "results"

[my_study_project]
my_study_workers = "wrangler, analyst"

[wrangler]
techniques = "load_court_listener, code_panels, cases_to_votes"

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = "courtlistener"
download = "bulk"
courts = "federal_circuits"
start_date = "2010-01-01"
rulebooks = "federal, review"
save = "cases.parquet"
reuse = true

[cases_to_votes_parameters]
label = "vote_reversal"
groups = "case_id"

Run it with courtpy run studies/my_study.toml, or with the study's own program (below). The Advanced User Guide lists every parameter of courtpy's loaders.

docs.title: A program of your own
docs.text:
courtpy.cli.main takes the study's commands, so the study's program has courtpy's commands and its own. In __main__.py:

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import sys
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Any

from courtpy import cli

from . import INSTRUCTIONS, measures


def main(argv: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> int:
    return cli.main(
        argv, prog = 'my-study', add_commands = _add_commands)


def _add_commands(commands: Any) -> None:
    scores = commands.add_parser('scores', help = 'score the judges')
    scores.add_argument('votes', help = 'a saved table of votes')
    scores.set_defaults(command = _scores)
    # The roster of judges codes their careers with the study's rules.
    commands.choices['judges'].set_defaults(
        rulebook = str(INSTRUCTIONS / 'careers.csv'))


def _scores(arguments: argparse.Namespace) -> int:
    measures.score(arguments.votes)
    return 0


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

Name the program in pyproject.toml:

[project.scripts]
my-study = "my_study.__main__:main"

Then my-study judges makes the roster of judges with the study's rules, my-study run studies/my_study.toml runs the study, and my-study scores runs the study's own command. Errors that a user can fix (a missing file, a missing column, a failed download) are shown as one line that starts with the program's name.

docs.title: Data that studies share
docs.text: courtpy keeps large downloads (the bulk data, the roster of judges, and the reference tables) in "courts" in the data folder of the amos workspace, outside of any one study, so every study uses the same files. Set COURTPY_DATA_DIR to keep them elsewhere (see Folders).

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial collects a small set of federal appellate cases from CourtListener, turns them into a table, and analyzes it. Each step can be run on its own, and each saves its work.

docs.title: The vocabulary
docs.text: Part What it is In code Case One decision: its sections of text (such as the parties, the judges, and the opinions) and information that needs no parsing (such as the date filed). courtpy.Case Rule One row of a CSV file that finds something in a section of text. amos.parsers.Rule Rulebook The rules of one or more CSV files, applied in order. amos.parsers.Rulebook (and courtpy's own in courtpy.rules) Case table A pandas.DataFrame with one row for each case. courtpy.parse Coder A technique that adds variables to the case table, such as whether a decision reversed the court below. courtpy.coders Project A study: the cases and an amos analysis of them. courtpy.Project

docs.title: 1. Collect cases
docs.text:
CourtListener offers its opinions in two ways. The bulk data needs no API key and has no limits, but its files are large (the opinions alone are more than 50 GB), so extracting cases takes a few hours. It is the best way to collect a large set of cases:

import courtpy

courtpy.BulkData().extract(
    courts = "ca1",
    start_date = "2019-01-01",
    end_date = "2019-12-31",
    folder = "courtlistener")

The API is faster for a small or very recent set of cases, but it needs an API key and limits how many requests an account can make. Get a key from the "API" page of your CourtListener profile and store it once, in a terminal:

courtpy key set

Then download:

courtpy.CourtListener().download(
    "ca1", "2026-09-01", "2026-09-30", "courtlistener", max_cases = 40)

Either way, each case is saved as a JSON file in a folder for its court, such as courtlistener/ca1/4567890.json. Running a download again skips the cases that were already saved.

docs.title: 2. Parse the cases into a table
docs.text:
courtpy.parse reads every saved case in a folder and applies the rules in the "federal" rulebook (see Writing Rules):

table = courtpy.parse("courtlistener")
print(table.shape)
print(table[["case_name", "court_num", "panel_judges", "disposition"]].head())

Each row is labeled by the case's CourtListener id. Among the columns are the parties (party1 and party2) and their roles (party1_appellant, party2_united_states, and so on), the judges (panel_judges, author, dissenting), the disposition (disposition_reverse, decision_reverse, and others), the issues the opinions discuss (criminal_firearm, civil_titlevii, constitutional_amend4, and many more), and the citations in the opinions (citations_case and others).

docs.title: 3. Code the outcomes
docs.text:
The coders add variables that combine others: whether each case is criminal, each party's role in the case, and the outcome of the appeal:

dataset = courtpy.code(table)
coded = dataset.data
print(coded["outcome_reversal"].mean())
print(coded[["type_criminal", "outcome_criminal_defendant_won"]].value_counts())

courtpy.code returns Cases, an amos.Dataset with one row for each case, whose history records each coder. Save it so that the steps above need not be repeated:

dataset.save("cases.csv")
dataset = courtpy.Cases.load("cases.csv")

The CSV file can be opened in a spreadsheet, and "cases.joblib" beside it holds the whole dataset (its label, history, and so on), which courtpy.Cases.load("cases.joblib") loads as it was. Columns with several values in a case (such as the judges) are text, with "; " between the values. The split_values coder turns them into lists, which are saved as text in the same way.

docs.title: 4. Analyze the table
docs.text:
courtpy.Project is amos.Project, so an analysis is described with amos settings. This one predicts reversals from a few features. (logit is scikit-learn's logistic regression; amos's logit_sm is the statsmodels model, with a table of coefficients, which needs pip install amos[statistics].)

settings = {
    "general": {"seed": 43, "label": "outcome_reversal"},
    "study_project": {"study_workers": "wrangler, explorer, analyst, critic"},
    "wrangler": {"techniques": "keep_columns, drop_missing"},
    "keep_columns_parameters": {
        "columns": ["year", "published", "type_criminal", "dissents",
                    "word_count", "criminal_firearm", "standard_de_novo"]},
    "explorer": {"techniques": "summarize, label_balance"},
    "analyst": {
        "design": "experiment",
        "criterion": "roc_auc",
        "steps": "split, model",
        "split_techniques": "stratified",
        "model_techniques": "baseline, logit"},
    "critic": {"techniques": "scorecard"},
}
project = courtpy.Project.create(settings, item = coded)
print(project.result.tables["scorecard"])
project.export()

export saves the report, the settings, the versions of every package, the history of every technique, and the tables and figures in a folder named for the run, so the study can be reported and reproduced.

docs.title: 5. Describe the whole study in one file
docs.text:
Steps 1 to 3 can be part of the study itself. courtpy's loaders are amos techniques that collect, parse, and code cases, so a project whose wrangler starts with one needs no other data. Save this as study.ini:

[general]
seed = 43
label = outcome_reversal

[study_project]
study_workers = wrangler, analyst, critic

[wrangler]
techniques = load_court_listener, keep_columns, drop_missing

[load_court_listener_parameters]
source = courtlistener
download = api
courts = ca1
start_date = 2026-09-01
end_date = 2026-09-30
max_cases = 40
save = cases.csv
reuse = true

[keep_columns_parameters]
columns = year, published, type_criminal, dissents, word_count

[analyst]
techniques = stratified, logit

[critic]
techniques = scorecard

and run it in a terminal:

courtpy run study.ini --export

The first run downloads, parses, and codes the cases and saves the table in cases.csv. Later runs reuse that file (because of reuse = true) and only repeat the analysis. The project's history records the loader and each coder, so the export shows exactly how the data was made. See examples/federal_appeals.ini for a fuller study.

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
Accessible tools for collecting, parsing, and analyzing court opinions

Contents

BulkData: extracts cases from CourtListener's bulk data. Case: the text and information of one case, ready to be parsed. CaseLoader: base class for techniques that load court cases. CaseTypes: a dataset with one row for each case type. Cases: a dataset with one row for each case. CourtData: base class for courtpy's datasets. CourtListener: downloads cases with the CourtListener API. Courts: a dataset with one row for each court. Dockets: a dataset with one row for each docket number of each case. Download: base class for a way to download cases, which a study can subclass to add its own. Judges: a dataset with one row for each judge. Parser: parses cases with rulebooks. PartyTypes: a dataset with one row for each party type. Project: an amos project, which runs a study from its settings. ReferenceLoader: base class for techniques that load reference data. Source: base class for a source of saved cases, which a study can subclass to add its own. SourceLoader: base class for techniques that download cases from a source and parse them. Votes: a dataset with one row for each judge on each case. code: applies coders to a table of parsed cases. parse: parses a folder of saved cases into a table.

docs.title: available(kind='opinions')
docs.text:
Returns the dates of the files of one kind in the bucket.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kind str

"courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or "opinions". Defaults to "opinions".

'opinions'

Returns:

Type Description list[str]

The dates, from oldest to newest.

Source code in src/courtpy/sources/bulk.py 
def available(self, kind: str = 'opinions') -> list[str]:
    """Returns the dates of the files of one kind in the bucket.

    Args:
        kind: "courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or
            "opinions". Defaults to "opinions".

    Returns:
        The dates, from oldest to newest.

    """
    dates = []
    for key in self._list(f'{options._BULK_PREFIX}{kind}-'):
        match = _DATE.search(key)
        # Skips files whose kind only starts with `kind` (such as
        # "opinions-cited" for "opinions").
        if match and key == (
            f'{options._BULK_PREFIX}{kind}-{match.group(1)}.csv.bz2'):
            dates.append(match.group(1))
    return sorted(set(dates))

docs.title: chunks(kind, *, columns=None, keep=None)
docs.text:
Yields chosen rows and columns of one bulk file, a chunk at a time.

The file is read with amos.loaders.read_chunks, which parses and decompresses it on every core and finds the rows in keep before any of their text becomes Python objects. If stream is true, the file is read from the bucket as it arrives, without being saved. Otherwise, it is downloaded first (or found in folder) with fetch.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default kind str

"courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or "opinions".

required columns Sequence[str] | None

the columns to return. Defaults to None, which returns every column.

None keep Mapping[str, Any] | None

the values to keep of each of some columns, such as {'court_id': ['ca1']} (see amos.loaders.read_chunks). Defaults to None, which keeps every row.

None

Yields:

Type Description DataFrame

pd.DataFrame: the rows of each chunk that are kept, with every value as text. Missing values are empty strs.

Source code in src/courtpy/sources/bulk.py 
def chunks(
    self,
    kind: str,
    *,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    keep: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> Iterator[pd.DataFrame]:
    """Yields chosen rows and columns of one bulk file, a chunk at a time.

    The file is read with `amos.loaders.read_chunks`, which parses and
    decompresses it on every core and finds the rows in `keep` before
    any of their text becomes Python objects. If `stream` is true, the
    file is read from the bucket as it arrives, without being saved.
    Otherwise, it is downloaded first (or found in `folder`) with
    `fetch`.

    Args:
        kind: "courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or
            "opinions".
        columns: the columns to return. Defaults to `None`, which
            returns every column.
        keep: the values to keep of each of some columns, such as
            `{'court_id': ['ca1']}` (see `amos.loaders.read_chunks`).
            Defaults to `None`, which keeps every row.

    Yields:
        pd.DataFrame: the rows of each chunk that are kept, with every
            value as text. Missing values are empty `str`s.

    """
    source = self._url(kind) if self.stream else self.fetch(kind)
    yield from amos.loaders.read_chunks(
        source,
        columns = columns,
        keep = keep,
        double_quote = False,
        escape_char = '\\',
        session = self.session,
        timeout = self.timeout)

Source code in src/courtpy/sources/bulk.py 
def extract(
    self,
    courts: str | Iterable[str],
    start_date: str | None = None,
    end_date: str | None = None,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str = 'courtlistener',
    *,
    max_cases: int | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Saves the cases of `courts` filed between two dates.

    Args:
        courts: CourtListener court ids (such as "ca1") or names of groups
            of them (such as "federal_appellate").
        start_date: earliest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None`
            (no earliest date).
        end_date: latest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None` (no
            latest date).
        folder: folder to save the cases in. Defaults to "courtlistener".
        max_cases: most cases to save. Defaults to `None` (every case).
        overwrite: whether to replace cases that were already saved with
            their opinions. Defaults to `False`.

    Returns:
        The paths of the cases saved (or updated) by this call.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder)
    wanted = utilities.expand_courts(courts)
    date = self.resolve_date()
    logger.info('extracting cases from the bulk data of %s', date)
    court_records = self._courts(wanted)
    docket_courts = self._docket_courts(set(wanted))
    clusters = self._clusters(
        docket_courts, start_date, end_date, max_cases)
    dockets = self._dockets(
        {int(c['docket_id']) for c in clusters.values()})
    citations = self._citations(set(clusters))
    paths: dict[int, pathlib.Path] = {}
    for cluster_id, cluster in clusters.items():
        docket = dockets[int(cluster['docket_id'])]
        court = docket_courts[int(cluster['docket_id'])]
        path = courtlistener.case_path(folder, court, cluster_id)
        if not overwrite and courtlistener.is_complete(path):
            continue
        courtlistener.save_case(path, {
            'source': 'courtlistener',
            'bulk_date': date,
            'court': court_records.get(court, {'id': court}),
            'cluster': cluster,
            'docket': docket,
            'citations': citations.get(cluster_id, []),
            'opinions': []})
        paths[cluster_id] = path
    logger.info('saved %d cases; now adding their opinions', len(paths))
    if paths:
        self._opinions(paths)
    return list(paths.values())

def fetch(self, kind: str) -> pathlib.Path:
    """Downloads one bulk file, resuming a download that was interrupted.

    The file is downloaded with `amos.loaders.download_file`, which
    writes it beside its path (with ".part" added) until it is whole, so
    a file in `folder` is always complete.

    Args:
        kind: "courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or
            "opinions".

    Raises:
        OSError: if the download stopped before the whole file arrived
            (run it again to resume).
        requests.HTTPError: if the file cannot be downloaded.

    Returns:
        The path of the downloaded file.

    """
    name = self._name(kind)
    assert isinstance(self.folder, pathlib.Path)  # noqa: S101
    path = self.folder / name
    if not path.is_file():
        logger.info('downloading %s to %s', name, self.folder)
    return amos.loaders.download_file(
        self._url(kind),
        path,
        timeout = self.timeout,
        session = self.session,
        resume = True)

def resolve_date(self) -> str:
    """Returns `date`, finding the newest complete set of files if needed.

    Returns:
        The date of the files to use, as YYYY-MM-DD.

    Raises:
        LookupError: if no date has every kind of file that courtpy needs.

    """
    if self.date is None:
        common: set[str] | None = None
        for kind in _KINDS:
            dates = set(self.available(kind))
            common = dates if common is None else common & dates
        if not common:
            message = 'no date in the bulk data has every file needed'
            raise LookupError(message)
        self.date = max(common)
    return self.date

def rows(
    self,
    kind: str,
    *,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    keep: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> Iterator[dict[str, str]]:
    """Yields chosen rows of one bulk file.

    Args:
        kind: "courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or
            "opinions".
        columns: the columns to return. Defaults to `None`, which
            returns every column.
        keep: the values to keep of each of some columns (see `chunks`).
            Defaults to `None`, which keeps every row.

    Yields:
        dict[str, str]: each row, mapping column names to text. Missing
            values are empty `str`s.

    """
    for chunk in self.chunks(kind, columns = columns, keep = keep):
        for row in chunk.to_dict('records'):
            yield {str(key): value for key, value in row.items()}

Bases: Loader, ABC

Base class for techniques that load court cases.

A subclass writes load, which collects and parses the cases at a source (a folder or file, already found with the clerk) and returns a table of them, one row for each case. apply then codes the table with the loader's "coders", saves it if "save" is set, and makes it the dataset that the rest of the workflow works on, with the label, task, and groups from the loader's parameters (which default to the "general" section of the settings). The label can be a column that a coder makes. If no coder makes it, it is pending, as in amos: a later technique (such as "derive_columns") can still make it, and using it before then raises an error. The dataset's history records the loader and then each coder.

The dataset is Cases, or the kind that the last of the coders makes (such as Votes, if "cases_to_votes" is the last). If "save" is set, it is saved with CourtData.save: whole, in a joblib file beside the table (such as "cases.joblib" beside "cases.csv"), and as the table. If "reuse" is true and it was saved before, the saved dataset is loaded instead (from the joblib file, or else from the table), and nothing is collected, parsed, or coded again.

def apply(self, item: amos.Dataset, **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Loads, codes, and saves the cases, as a dataset continuing `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset so far, whose seed and history are kept.
        **kwargs: "source", "coders", "save", "reuse", "label", "task", and
            "groups", and parameters for `load`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if there is no "source" and the loader has no default
            source.

    Returns:
        The dataset of the coded cases.

    """
    source = kwargs.pop('source', None) or self.default_source
    if source is None:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} has nothing to load: set its "source" in the '
            f'"{self.name}_parameters" section of the settings'
        )
        raise ValueError(message)
    label = kwargs.pop('label', None) or item.label
    task = kwargs.pop('task', None)
    groups = kwargs.pop('groups', None) or item.groups or None
    names = kwargs.pop('coders', self.default_coders)
    save = kwargs.pop('save', None)
    reuse = utilities.to_bool(kwargs.pop('reuse', False))
    saved = self._interim(save) if save else None
    reused = _reusable(saved) if saved is not None and reuse else None
    dataset: amos.Dataset
    if reused is not None:
        dataset = LoadCases().load(reused)
        dataset.seed = item.seed
        dataset.history = [*item.history, *dataset.history]
        dataset.record(
            self.name, source = str(source), reused = str(reused),
            rows = len(dataset.data), columns = len(dataset.data.columns))
    else:
        loaded = self.load(self._locate(source), **kwargs)
        if isinstance(loaded, amos.Dataset):
            dataset = loaded
            dataset.seed = item.seed
            dataset.history = [*item.history, *dataset.history]
        else:
            dataset = datasets.Cases(data = loaded, seed = item.seed)
            dataset.history = item.history
        dataset.record(
            self.name, source = str(source), rows = len(dataset.data),
            columns = len(dataset.data.columns))
        dataset = coders.code(dataset, names)
        if saved is not None and isinstance(dataset, datasets.CourtData):
            dataset.save(saved, clerk = self._get_clerk())
    return type(dataset).create(
        dataset, label = label, task = task, groups = groups)

@classmethod
def adopt(cls, dataset: amos.Dataset) -> Self:
    """Returns `dataset` as a dataset of this kind.

    The new dataset shares everything with `dataset` (its data, label,
    split, history, and so on), so a shaper can hand on a dataset of
    another kind. If the data has a column named `key`, it labels the
    rows.

    Args:
        dataset: a dataset of any kind.

    Returns:
        `dataset` itself if it is already of this kind, and otherwise a
            new dataset of this kind with the same attributes.

    """
    if type(dataset) is cls:
        adopted = dataset
    else:
        adopted = cls.__new__(cls)
        adopted.__dict__.update(dataset.__dict__)
    adopted._label_rows()
    return adopted

@classmethod
def load(cls, path: pathlib.Path | str, **kwargs: Any) -> Self:
    """Loads a dataset that `save` saved, or a table of one.

    A joblib file holds the whole dataset, which goes on from where it
    was saved. A table (such as a CSV or parquet file) holds only its
    data: the column named `key` labels the rows again, and columns of
    booleans and whole numbers with missing values get the types that
    allow them (see `cases.tidy`).

    Args:
        path: the path of the file.
        **kwargs: arguments of `amos.Dataset.create`, such as "label"
            and "groups".

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if there is no file at `path`.
        TypeError: if the file holds a courtpy dataset of another kind.

    Returns:
        The dataset.

    """
    path = pathlib.Path(path).expanduser()
    if not path.is_file():
        message = f'there is no file of {cls.__name__} at {path}'
        raise FileNotFoundError(message)
    loaded = amos.Dataset.create(path, **kwargs)
    if isinstance(loaded, CourtData) and not isinstance(loaded, cls):
        message = (
            f'{path} holds {type(loaded).__name__}, not {cls.__name__}: '
            f'load it with courtpy.{type(loaded).__name__}.load'
        )
        raise TypeError(message)
    dataset = loaded if isinstance(loaded, cls) else cls.adopt(loaded)
    if not isinstance(loaded, CourtData):
        dataset.data = cases.tidy(dataset.data)
        dataset._label_rows()
    return dataset

def save(
    self,
    path: pathlib.Path | str,
    *,
    clerk: nagata.FileManager | None = None,
    compress: int | bool = 0) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Saves the whole dataset, and its data as a table.

    The `save_data` technique of `amos` saves the dataset in a joblib file
    named for `path` (such as "cases.joblib" beside "cases.csv"), which
    `load` loads as it was, and the data in `path`, in the format of its
    extension: ".csv", ".parquet", or ".xlsx". A path ending in ".joblib"
    (or with no extension) saves only the dataset. Several values in one
    cell (such as the lists that `split_values` makes) are saved as text,
    with "; " between them, as courtpy's rules write them. The dataset's
    history records where the files are.

    Args:
        path: the path of the table. Its folder is made if needed.
        clerk: the file manager that saves the files. Defaults to `None`,
            in which case one for the folder of `path` is used, so
            nothing else is made.
        compress: how much joblib compresses the file of the dataset,
            from 0 (not at all) to 9. Defaults to 0.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the extension of `path` is not one listed above.

    Returns:
        The paths of the files that were saved.

    """
    path = pathlib.Path(path).expanduser().resolve()
    suffix = path.suffix.lower()
    if suffix not in _TABLE_FORMATS:
        message = (
            f'{path.name} must end in one of '
            f'{[s for s in _TABLE_FORMATS if s]}')
        raise ValueError(message)
    folder = path.parent
    folder.mkdir(parents = True, exist_ok = True)
    if clerk is None:
        clerk = nagata.FileManager(
            root_folder = folder,
            input_folder = folder,
            interim_folder = folder,
            output_folder = folder)
    joined = copy.copy(self)
    joined.data = _join_lists(self.data)
    joined.history = list(self.history)
    amos.savers.SaveData(clerk = clerk).apply(
        joined,
        folder = folder,
        file_name = path.stem,
        table_format = _TABLE_FORMATS[suffix] or False,
        compress = compress)
    self.history.append(joined.history[-1])
    return [pathlib.Path(file) for file in joined.history[-1]['files']]

Every request includes the API key, which is found with courtpy.secrets.get_api_key if it is not passed. Requests are spaced at least min_interval seconds apart.     overwrite: bool = False) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the cases of `courts` filed between two dates.

    Each page of cases (opinion clusters) takes one request, and their
    opinions take one more (or more, if they have many opinions). Cases
    that were already saved (with their opinions) are skipped, and the
    place in each court's list of cases is saved, so running a download
    again resumes it. Running a finished download again takes one request
    for each court and saves any cases added to CourtListener since.

    Args:
        courts: CourtListener court ids (such as "ca1") or names of groups
            of them (such as "federal_appellate").
        start_date: earliest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None`
            (no earliest date).
        end_date: latest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None` (no
            latest date).
        folder: folder to save the cases in. Defaults to "courtlistener".
        max_cases: most cases to save in each court in this run. Defaults
            to `None` (every case).
        dockets: whether to also download each case's docket (every
            field but those in `options._DOCKET_SKIPPED`, such as its
            docket number, dates, and the court appealed from). This
            takes one more request for each case. Defaults to `False`.
            The bulk data always includes the docket.
        overwrite: whether to download cases that were already saved.
            Defaults to `False`.

    Raises:
        RateLimitError: if CourtListener asks for a pause longer than
            `max_wait`. What was downloaded is kept.

    Returns:
        The paths of the cases saved in this run.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder)
    saved: list[pathlib.Path] = []
    for court in utilities.expand_courts(courts):
        saved.extend(self._download_court(
            court, start_date, end_date, folder,
            max_cases = max_cases, dockets = dockets,
            overwrite = overwrite))
    logger.info(
        'saved %d cases in %s with %d requests', len(saved), folder,
        self.requests_made)
    return saved

def get(
    self,
    path: str,
    params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Returns the JSON response of one request to the API.

    Args:
        path: a path in the API (such as "clusters/") or a full address
            (such as the "next" page of a response).
        params: query parameters. Defaults to `None`.

    Raises:
        CourtListenerError: if the API returns an error, rejects the key,
            or cannot be reached after several tries.
        RateLimitError: if the API asks for a pause longer than
            `max_wait`.

    Returns:
        The decoded JSON.

    """
    url = path if path.startswith('http') else urllib.parse.urljoin(
        self.base_url, path)
    failures = 0
    while True:
        self._space_requests()
        try:
            response = self.session.get(
                url, params = params, timeout = self.timeout)
        except requests.RequestException as error:
            failures += 1
            if failures > _RETRIES:
                message = f'CourtListener could not be reached: {error}'
                raise CourtListenerError(message) from error
            time.sleep(5 * 2 ** failures)
            continue
        finally:
            self.requests_made += 1
            self._last_request = time.monotonic()
        status = response.status_code
        if status == 429:
            wait = _retry_after(response)
            if wait > self.max_wait:
                raise RateLimitError(wait)
            logger.info(
                'CourtListener asked for a pause: waiting %.0f seconds',
                wait)
            time.sleep(wait)
            continue
        if status in _TEMPORARY and failures < _RETRIES:
            failures += 1
            time.sleep(5 * 2 ** failures)
            continue
        if status in (401, 403):
            message = (
                f'CourtListener rejected the request ({status}). Check '
                f'the API key with "courtpy key show". Details: '
                f'{_detail(response)}'
            )
            raise CourtListenerError(message)
        if status >= 400:
            message = (
                f'CourtListener returned {status}: {_detail(response)}')
            raise CourtListenerError(message)
        return dict(response.json())

def pages(
    self,
    path: str,
    params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> Iterator[
        tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], str | None]]:
    """Yields the results of each page of a list, and the next address.

    Args:
        path: a path in the API (such as "clusters/") or the address of a
            page.
        params: query parameters for the first page. Defaults to `None`.

    Yields:
        tuple[list[dict[str, Any]], str | None]: the results on each page
            and the address of the next page (or `None` after the last
            page).

    """
    url: str | None = path
    query = params
    while url:
        data = self.get(url, query)
        next_url = data.get('next')
        yield list(data.get('results', [])), next_url
        url, query = next_url, None

@classmethod
def create(
    cls,
    rulebooks: str | pathlib.Path | Sequence[str | pathlib.Path] = (
        options._DEFAULT_JURISDICTION),
    *,
    keep_text: bool = False) -> Parser:
    """Returns a parser with the rules in `rulebooks`.

    The rules of `options._REQUIRED_RULEBOOKS` are always applied first
    (after the header rules of each case's source), whether or not they
    are named.

    Args:
        rulebooks: names of rulebooks (such as "federal" or "civil") or
            paths to CSV files or folders of them, applied in order.
            Defaults to `options._DEFAULT_JURISDICTION`.
        keep_text: whether to keep the text of the cases' sections in the
            table. Defaults to `False`.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if a rulebook is not the name of one, a CSV
            file, or a folder with CSV files.
        ValueError: if a file is missing a column or a row is not a valid
            rule. The message names the file and row.

    Returns:
        The parser.

    """
    if isinstance(rulebooks, str):
        rulebooks = utilities.listify(rulebooks)
    elif isinstance(rulebooks, pathlib.Path):
        rulebooks = [rulebooks]
    rulebook = amos.parsers.Rulebook.create(
        *options._REQUIRED_RULEBOOKS, *rulebooks)
    return cls(rulebook = rulebook, keep_text = keep_text)

def parse_cases(self, found: Sequence[cases.Case]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns a table of `found`, with a row for each case.

    The cases of each source are parsed together, with every rule
    searching every case at once.

    Args:
        found: the cases to parse.

    Returns:
        The table, with a row for each case, in order, labeled 0, 1, 2,
            and so on. Information from a case's `metadata` comes first
            and is used instead of any variable of the same name that the
            rules find (unless it is missing).

    """
    groups: dict[str, list[int]] = {}
    for position, case in enumerate(found):
        groups.setdefault(case.source, []).append(position)
    tables = [
        self._parse_source([found[p] for p in positions]).set_axis(
            positions)
        for positions in groups.values()]
    if not tables:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    return pd.concat(tables).sort_index() if len(tables) > 1 else tables[0]

def find_files(self, folder: pathlib.Path | str) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Returns the saved cases in a folder and its subfolders.

    Args:
        folder: the folder.

    Returns:
        The paths of the files that match `pattern`, sorted. Files in
            hidden folders (such as ".courtpy", where downloads keep
            their place) are left out.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder)
    return sorted(
        p for p in folder.rglob(self.pattern)
        if p.is_file() and not any(
            part.startswith('.') for part in p.relative_to(folder).parts))

def load(
    self,
    source: Any,
    *,
    download: Any = None,
    courts: Any = None,
    start_date: Any = None,
    end_date: Any = None,
    max_cases: Any = None,
    overwrite: Any = False,
    rulebooks: Any = None,
    keep_text: Any = False,
    limit: Any = None,
    workers: Any = None,
    **options: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Downloads the cases (if asked) and parses the folder `source`.

    Settings can be text (as a settings file gives them), so each is
    converted to the type it needs.

    Args:
        source: the folder of saved cases, found with the clerk.
        download: the name of a way to download, or "none". Defaults to
            `None` (none).
        courts: CourtListener court ids or groups to download. Defaults
            to `None`.
        start_date: earliest date filed to download (YYYY-MM-DD).
            Defaults to `None`.
        end_date: latest date filed to download (YYYY-MM-DD). Defaults
            to `None`.
        max_cases: most cases to download. Defaults to `None` (every
            case).
        overwrite: whether to download cases that were already saved.
            Defaults to `False`.
        rulebooks: rules to parse with. Defaults to `None`, in which case
            `options._DEFAULT_JURISDICTION` is used.
        keep_text: whether to keep the text of the cases' sections.
            Defaults to `False`.
        limit: most cases to parse. Defaults to `None` (every case).
        workers: number of processes to parse with. Defaults to `None`
            (one).
        **options: options of the way to download, such as "bulk_date".
            A folder or file that one names (such as "bulk_folder") is
            found with the clerk.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if "download" names no way to download, or one that
            saves cases of another source, or if no cases are found.

    Returns:
        The table of parsed cases, labeled by "case_id".

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(source)
    if not utilities.is_none_setting(download):
        method = base.find_download(str(download))
        if method.source != self.reads:
            message = (
                f'the "{method.name}" download saves {method.source} '
                f'cases, but {self.name!r} reads {self.reads} cases')
            raise ValueError(message)
        method(locate = self._locate).download(
            folder,
            courts = utilities.expand_courts(courts) if courts else None,
            start_date = utilities.to_date(start_date),
            end_date = utilities.to_date(end_date),
            max_cases = utilities.to_integer(max_cases),
            overwrite = utilities.to_bool(overwrite),
            **options)
    return _parse(
        folder, self.reads, rulebooks = rulebooks,
        keep_text = keep_text, limit = limit, workers = workers)

def code(
    data: pd.DataFrame | amos.Dataset,
    coders: str | Sequence[str] | None = options._DEFAULT_CODERS,
    *,
    parameters: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Applies coders (or other `amos` techniques) to parsed cases.

    Args:
        data: the parsed cases, or a dataset of them (which is changed in
            place).
        coders: names of the techniques to apply, in order. Defaults to
            `options._DEFAULT_CODERS`. "none" (or `None`) applies none.
        parameters: parameters for the techniques, by their names. Defaults
            to `None`.

    Returns:
        A dataset of the coded cases, whose history records each technique:
            `Cases` made from a table, or the kind that the last shaper made
            (such as `Votes`, after "cases_to_votes").

    """
    dataset = (
        data if isinstance(data, amos.Dataset)
        else datasets.Cases.create(data))
    for name in utilities.listify(coders):
        if utilities.is_none_setting(name):
            continue
        kind = cast(
            'type[amos.Operation]',
            chrisjen.library.borrow(name, genre = 'operation'))
        settings = dict((parameters or {}).get(name, {}))
        technique = kind(parameters = settings)
        dataset = technique.apply(dataset)
    return dataset

def parse(
    files: pathlib.Path | str | Iterable[pathlib.Path | str],
    source: str = 'courtlistener',
    rulebooks: str | pathlib.Path | Sequence[str | pathlib.Path] = (
        options._DEFAULT_JURISDICTION),
    *,
    keep_text: bool = False,
    limit: int | None = None,
    workers: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Parses saved cases into a table, one row for each case.

    Columns with several values in a case (such as "panel_judges" and
    "citations_case") are text, with "; " between the values. The
    `split_values` technique (`coders.SplitValues`) turns them into lists or
    into a column for each value.

    Args:
        files: a folder of saved cases (searched with its subfolders), or the
            paths of saved cases.
        source: the name of the source the cases came from, such as
            "courtlistener" (the default) or "lexis_nexis" (see
            `courtpy.sources.SOURCES`).
        rulebooks: names of rulebooks (such as "federal") or paths to CSV
            files or folders of them. Defaults to
            `options._DEFAULT_JURISDICTION`.
        keep_text: whether to keep the text of the cases' sections in the
            table (see `ParseAll`). Defaults to `False`.
        limit: most cases to parse, for trying out rules. Defaults to `None`
            (every case).
        workers: number of processes to parse with. Defaults to 1.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if there is no source named `source`.

    Returns:
        The table, labeled by each case's id ("case_id"). A case that cannot
            be read is left out, with a warning.

    """
    reader = base.find_source(source)
    if isinstance(files, str | pathlib.Path):
        paths = reader.find_files(files)
    else:
        paths = [pathlib.Path(p) for p in files]
    if limit is not None:
        paths = paths[:limit]
    parser = Parser.create(rulebooks, keep_text = keep_text)
    labels: list[str] = []
    tables: list[pd.DataFrame] = []
    failures = 0
    outcomes: list[Any] = []
    for chunk_outcomes, table in _parse_all(parser, paths, reader, workers):
        outcomes.extend(chunk_outcomes)
        tables.append(table)
    taken: set[str] = set()
    for path, outcome in zip(paths, outcomes, strict = True):
        if isinstance(outcome, BaseException):
            failures += 1
            logger.warning('%s could not be parsed: %s', path, outcome)
            continue
        unique, number = outcome, 1
        while unique in taken:
            number += 1
            unique = f'{outcome}_{number}'
        taken.add(unique)
        labels.append(unique)
    logger.info(
        'parsed %d cases (%d could not be parsed)', len(labels), failures)
    tables = [t for t in tables if not t.empty]
    data = pd.concat(tables, ignore_index = True) if tables else pd.DataFrame()
    data.index = pd.Index(labels, name = 'case_id')
    return cases.tidy(data)

docs.text:
Command line interface for courtpy.

Run courtpy --help (or courtpy {command} --help) in a terminal for help.

Command Does courtpy key set Stores your CourtListener API key outside of any project. courtpy key show Shows where your key is found (with most of it hidden). courtpy key delete Removes your stored key. courtpy download bulk Extracts cases from CourtListener's bulk data (no key needed). courtpy download api Downloads cases with the CourtListener API (a key is needed). courtpy download {way} Downloads cases in a way that a study adds (see courtpy.sources.Download). courtpy split Divides Lexis-Nexis files of many cases into one file per case. courtpy parse Parses saved cases into a table (a CSV or parquet file). courtpy rules Checks a rulebook and lists the variables it makes. courtpy judges Makes and saves the roster of judges from the Federal Judicial Center's files. courtpy run Collects, parses, and analyzes cases as a settings file describes.

Each command is a private function that takes the parsed arguments and returns the program's exit code (0 for success). _parser connects each command's name to its function.

A study built on courtpy can have a program of its own with courtpy's commands and its own, by passing a function that adds them to main:

def main(argv: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> int:
    return courtpy.cli.main(
        argv, prog = 'my-study', add_commands = _add_commands)


def _add_commands(commands: Any) -> None:
    scores = commands.add_parser('scores', help = 'score the judges')
    scores.add_argument('votes')
    scores.set_defaults(command = _scores)
    # The study's own rules for the judges' careers.
    commands.choices['judges'].set_defaults(rulebook = CAREERS)
Contents

main: runs a command. _DOWNLOAD_SHARED: the arguments of "courtpy download" that are not options of a way to download.

def main(
    argv: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    *,
    prog: str = 'courtpy',
    description: str | None = None,
    add_commands: Callable[[Any], None] | None = None) -> int:
    """Runs a courtpy command, or a command that a study adds.

    Messages about progress are shown unless "--quiet" is passed. Errors that
    a user can fix (such as a missing API key, a misspelled file, an invalid
    rule, or a failed download) are shown as one line instead of a
    traceback.

    Args:
        argv: the command's arguments. Defaults to `None`, in which case the
            arguments of the program are used.
        prog: the name of the program, for help and error messages. Defaults
            to "courtpy".
        description: what the program does, for its help. Defaults to
            `None`, which describes courtpy.
        add_commands: a function that adds commands to the program's
            subparsers (an `argparse` "subparsers" object, whose `choices`
            has courtpy's commands by name). Each command's "command" default
            is the function that runs it, which takes the parsed arguments
            and returns the exit code. Defaults to `None`, which adds none.

    Returns:
        0 if the command succeeded, and 1 if it failed.

    """
    parser = _parser(
        prog = prog, description = description, add_commands = add_commands)
    arguments = parser.parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(
        level = logging.WARNING if arguments.quiet else logging.INFO,
        format = '%(levelname)s: %(message)s')
    try:
        return int(arguments.command(arguments) or 0)
    except (
        courtlistener.CourtListenerError,
        secrets.MissingAPIKeyError,
        LookupError,
        OSError,
        ValueError,
        requests.RequestException) as error:
        print(f'{prog}: {error}', file = sys.stderr)
        return 1
