def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    source: Any = None,
    columns: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    prefix: str | None = 'judge_score_',
    on: str = 'judge_nid',
    other_on: str | None = None,
    numbered: bool | None = None,
    duplicates: str = 'error',
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Adds the scores of each judge of each row of `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of votes or of cases.
        source: the table of scores, or the path of a data file of one.
        columns: the scores to add. Defaults to `None`, for every column
            of the table but its key.
        prefix: text to put before the names of the added columns.
            Defaults to "judge_score_".
        on: the column of `item` with each judge's key, or (numbered) the
            start of the names of the columns of each seat's key.
            Defaults to "judge_nid".
        other_on: the column of the table with each judge's key.
            Defaults to `None`, for "judge_nid" or "nid" if the table has
            one, and otherwise `on`.
        numbered: whether each row has several judges, whose columns are
            numbered by their seats. Defaults to `None`, in which case it
            is true if `item` is `Cases`.
        duplicates: what to do if the table has several rows for a judge
            (see `amos.mergers.MergeKeys.match`). Defaults to "error".
        **kwargs: other parameters of `merge_keys`, such as "reader" and
            "indicator".

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `item` lacks the judges' keys, or the table lacks
            its key or one of `columns`.
        ValueError: if there is no `source`, or an added column would
            have the name of a column of the data.

    Returns:
        The dataset with the added columns.

    """
    if numbered is None:
        numbered = isinstance(item, datasets.Cases)
    if not numbered:
        other = _unlabeled(self.read(source)) if source is not None else (
            None)
        return super().apply(
            item,
            source = other if other is not None else source,
            columns = None if columns is None else utilities.listify(
                columns),
            prefix = prefix,
            on = on,
            other_on = other_on or _key_of(other, on),
            duplicates = duplicates,
            **kwargs)
    if source is None:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} has nothing to merge: set its "source" in the '
            f'"{self.name}_parameters" section of the settings')
        raise ValueError(message)
    other = _unlabeled(
        self.read(source, **dict(kwargs.pop('reader', None) or {})))
    key = other_on or _key_of(other, on)
    data = item.data
    pattern = re.compile(rf'{re.escape(on)}(\d+)')
    seats = sorted(
        int(numbered_column.group(1)) for column in data.columns
        if (numbered_column := pattern.fullmatch(str(column))))
    if not seats:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} needs the columns "{on}1", "{on}2", and so on, '
            f'with the key of the judge in each seat: apply "code_panels" '
            f'or "add_biography" first')
        raise KeyError(message)
    chosen = (
        [c for c in other.columns if c != key] if columns is None
        else utilities.listify(columns))
    cases.require_columns(
        other, [key, *chosen], 'the table of ' + repr(self.name))
    added: dict[str, Any] = {}
    matched = 0
    for seat in seats:
        positions = np.asarray(self.match(
            data, other, on = f'{on}{seat}', other_on = key,
            duplicates = duplicates), dtype = 'int64')
        matched += int((positions >= 0).sum())
        found = other[chosen].reset_index(drop = True).reindex(positions)
        for column in chosen:
            added[f'{prefix or ""}{column}{seat}'] = found[
                column].to_numpy()
    table = pd.DataFrame(added, index = data.index)
    clashes = [c for c in table.columns if c in data.columns]
    if clashes:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} would add columns named {clashes}, which the '
            f'data already has: set "prefix" to tell them apart')
        raise ValueError(message)
    item.replace(pd.concat([data, table], axis = 1))
    item.record(
        self.name,
        source = (
            type(source).__name__ if isinstance(source, pd.DataFrame)
            else str(source)),
        rows = len(data),
        matched = matched,
        created = list(table.columns))
    return item

docs.title: judges
docs.text:
Identifies the judges in parsed cases and adds what is known about them.

The federal rules find the names of the judges on each case as the opinion writes them, such as "LYNCH" and "R THOMPSON" (the "panel_judges", "authors", "concurring", and "dissenting" columns, with "; " between the names). To study the judges, each name has to be matched to a person. A Roster is a table of judges, with one row for each court that a judge has served on, which finds the judge that a name refers to from the court and year of the case.

build_roster makes that table with the fjc-biographies package (https://github.com/WithPrecedent/fjc_biographies), from three files of the Federal Judicial Center's Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges (which download gets with it): the judges' service on each court, their demographics, and their careers before the bench. The rules in its "judges" rulebook code the careers, and another rulebook can be named, so they can be changed without changing courtpy. fjc-biographies also adds scores of the judges' ideology, which it gets from the judicial-common-space package (https://github.com/WithPrecedent/judicial_common_space): each appointment's Judicial Common Space score ("jcs") and the justices' Martin-Quinn scores ("mq_first", "mq_last", "mq_mean", and "mq_terms"):

import courtpy

roster = courtpy.judges.Roster.from_fjc(jcs = True, martin_quinn = True)
roster.save()

A saved roster is kept outside of projects (in "judges" in courtpy.utilities.data_folder()), where the techniques look for it when no roster is named. It is a CSV file, so judges and columns (such as a score of each judge's ideology) can be added to it in a spreadsheet. Every column of numbers or booleans that does not identify or date a judge's service is an attribute of the judge, which the techniques use.

These techniques use a roster or the tables that it makes. They are added to the amos library as soon as courtpy is imported, so they can be named in settings. Cases and judges are different things, so the techniques are built from the mergers and shapers of amos, which join tables whose rows are not the same:

  • add_biography (an amos.Merger) adds what the roster says about each judge that each row names. Each row of Votes gets "judge_party", "judge_woman", and so on, and each row of Cases gets them for each seat of its panel: "judge_name1", "judge_party1", "judge_woman1", and so on for the first judge, "judge_name2" and the rest for the second.
  • add_jcs (an amos.Merger) is add_biography for each judge's Judicial Common Space score alone ("judge_jcs", or "judge_jcs1" and so on).
  • add_circuit (an amos.Merger) adds the median and total of the parties of the appointing presidents, and of the Judicial Common Space scores, of the active (not senior) judges of each case's circuit on the day it was decided.
  • code_panels (an amos.Munger) adds the composition of each case's panel: the share of its judges who are women, the mean party of the presidents who appointed them, and so on. It makes a row for each judge on each case (with lists_to_rows), finds the judges (with add_biography), and adds summaries of each case's judges to the case (with merge_summary).
  • cases_to_votes (an amos.Shaper) makes Votes: a table with one row for each judge on each case, with the judge's attributes, those of the other judges on the panel, and how the judge voted.
  • dockets_to_votes (an amos.Shaper) is cases_to_votes for Dockets: a row for each judge on each docket.
  • votes_to_cases (an amos.Shaper) undoes cases_to_votes: it makes Votes Cases again.
  • cases_to_judges (an amos.Shaper) makes Judges: a table with one row for each judge, which summarizes the judge's votes (with group_rows).
  • load_roster and download_biographies (reference loaders, see courtpy.loaders.ReferenceLoader) start a study of the judges themselves with a saved roster or one made from the Federal Judicial Center's files.

The parts are in private modules: _names (how names are compared), _roster (the roster and its loaders), _biographies (AddBiography and AddJcs), _circuits (AddCircuit), and _panels (the techniques for panels and votes).

Contents

AddBiography: adds what a roster says about each judge that each row names. AddCircuit: adds the ideology of the active judges of each case's circuit when the case was decided. AddJcs: adds the Judicial Common Space score of each judge that each row names. CasesToJudges: makes a table with one row for each judge. CasesToVotes: makes a table with one row for each judge on each case. CodePanels: adds the judges and the composition of each case's panel. DocketsToVotes: makes a table with one row for each judge on each docket. DownloadBiographies: downloads the Federal Judicial Center's files about judges and loads the roster that they make. LoadRoster: loads the table of a roster of judges. Roster: a table of judges that finds the judge a name refers to. VotesToCases: makes a table of votes a table of cases again. build_roster: makes the table of a roster from the Federal Judicial Center's files with fjc-biographies. clean_name: returns a name the way that names are compared. download: downloads the Federal Judicial Center's files about judges with fjc-biographies. name_forms: returns the ways that an opinion may write a judge's name, grouped by how much of the name they give. panel_compositions: returns the composition of each case's panel by the parties of the presidents who appointed its judges, such as "DDR". shorter_names: returns shorter ways of writing a name that an opinion gives, to try when the name itself fits no judge. republican_appointees: returns how many judges of each case's panel a Republican president appointed. vote_table: returns a table with one row for each judge on each case.

Bases: Merger

Adds what a roster says about each judge that each row names.

A name, as an opinion writes it (such as "LYNCH"), is matched to a judge in a roster (see Roster) with the court and year of the row's case, and the columns of the judge's row of the roster are added, with a prefix before their names. A name that is not matched gets missing values.

In Votes (or any table with a row for each judge), each row names one judge ("judge"), so it gets "judge_party", "judge_woman", and so on. With "name" set to "author" and "prefix" to "author_", a table of cases gets what is known about the author of each opinion.

In Cases, each case names several judges ("panel_judges", with "; " between the names), so the columns are numbered by each judge's seat (the place of the judge's name in the list): "judge_name1" (the judge's name, as the roster reports it), "judge_nid1" (the Federal Judicial Center's number for the judge), "judge_party1", "judge_woman1", and so on for the first judge, "judge_name2" and the rest for the second, for as many seats as the longest panel has. A name that is not matched leaves its seat missing, so the judges after it keep theirs. "judge_name" and "judge_nid" columns that the cases already have (from code_panels) are left as they are.

Instead of a roster, "lookup" can be a function that takes a judge's name (as the opinion writes it), the number of the case's court, and its year, and returns what is known about the judge, by the names of its columns (or None if nothing is). Then "judge_name1" is the name as the opinion writes it.

Like every merger of amos, it takes these parameters, never adds, removes, or reorders rows, and records how many rows it matched in the dataset's history:

Parameter Meaning source The roster: the path of a saved one (looked for in the current folder and then in the clerk's input folder), a roster, or the table of one. Without it, the roster saved in "judges" in utilities.data_folder() is used. columns The columns to add. By default, they are the roster's attributes (see Roster.attributes) and those that depend on the case: "age", "senior", "designated", and "district_judge" (see Roster.describe). All of them are added as numbers (1 and 0 for true and false). Any other column of the roster can be named too, such as "judge" (the judge's name, as the roster reports it), "nid", or "president". prefix Text to put before the names of the added columns. It is "judge_" unless another is set. indicator The name of a column to make that says whether each row's judge was found (or, numbered, how many of its judges were). name, court, year The columns of the data with the judges' names and the number of the court and the year of the row's case. They are "panel_judges" (for Cases) or "judge", "court_num", and "year" unless others are set. numbered Whether each row names several judges, whose columns are numbered by their seats. Unless it is set, it is true for Cases without a "name", and false otherwise. lookup A function that finds what is known about a judge, used instead of a roster.

def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    source: Any = None,
    columns: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    prefix: str | None = 'judge_',
    indicator: str | None = None,
    name: str | None = None,
    court: str = 'court_num',
    year: str = 'year',
    numbered: bool | None = None,
    lookup: Lookup | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Adds the columns of each judge that each row of `item` names.

    Args:
        item: the dataset to add columns to.
        source: the roster: a roster, the table of one, or the path of a
            saved one. Defaults to `None`, in which case the roster saved
            in "judges" in `utilities.data_folder()` is used. It is not
            used with `lookup`.
        columns: the columns to add: attributes of the judge (see
            `Roster.described`) or other columns of the roster (or, with
            `lookup`, names that it returns). Defaults to `None`, in
            which case they are every attribute (or, with `lookup`, every
            name that it returns).
        prefix: text to put before the names of the added columns.
            Defaults to "judge_".
        indicator: name of a column to make that says whether each row's
            judge was found, or (numbered) how many of its judges were.
            Defaults to `None`, which makes no such column.
        name: the column of `item` with the judges' names, as an opinion
            writes them. Defaults to `None`, in which case it is
            "panel_judges" if `numbered`, and otherwise "judge".
        court: the column of `item` with the number of the court of the
            row's case. Defaults to "court_num".
        year: the column of `item` with the year of the row's case.
            Defaults to "year".
        numbered: whether each row names several judges, separated by
            "; " (or in a list), whose columns are numbered by their
            seats. Defaults to `None`, in which case it is true if `item`
            is `Cases` and `name` is `None`.
        lookup: a function that takes a judge's name, the number of the
            case's court, and its year, and returns what is known about
            the judge (or `None`). Defaults to `None`, in which case the
            roster is used.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `item` lacks one of the columns `name`, `court`, and
            `year`, or one of `columns` is not in the roster.
        ValueError: if an added column would have the name of a column
            of the data.

    Returns:
        The dataset with the added columns. Its rows and index are not
            changed.

    """
    if numbered is None:
        numbered = isinstance(item, datasets.Cases) and name is None
    if name is None:
        name = 'panel_judges' if numbered else 'judge'
    if columns is None and self.default_columns is not None:
        columns = list(self.default_columns)
    data = item.data
    cases.require_columns(data, [name, court, year], repr(self.name))
    named = _listed(data, name, court, year) if numbered else pd.DataFrame({
        _ROW: np.arange(len(data)),
        _SEAT: 1,
        _WRITTEN: data[name].to_numpy(),
        court: data[court].to_numpy(),
        year: data[year].to_numpy()})
    if lookup is None:
        roster = self._roster(source)
        found, rows = self._from_roster(
            named, roster, columns, court = court, year = year)
        matched = rows >= 0
        identity = pd.DataFrame({
            'name': roster.data['judge'].reindex(rows).to_numpy(),
            'nid': roster.data['nid'].reindex(rows).astype(
                'Int64').array})
    else:
        found = _from_lookup(named, lookup, columns, court, year)
        matched = found.notna().any(axis = 1).to_numpy()
        identity = pd.DataFrame({
            'name': named[_WRITTEN].where(matched).to_numpy()})
    start = prefix or ''
    if numbered:
        identity = identity[[
            key for key in identity.columns
            if f'{start}{key}1' not in data.columns]]
        seated = pd.concat([
            named[[_ROW, _SEAT]].reset_index(drop = True),
            identity.add_prefix(start),
            found.add_prefix(start)], axis = 1)
        added = by_seat(seated, len(data))
        if indicator is not None:
            added[indicator] = pd.Series(matched).groupby(
                named[_ROW].to_numpy()).sum().reindex(
                    range(len(data)), fill_value = 0).to_numpy()
    else:
        added = found.add_prefix(start)
        if indicator is not None:
            added[indicator] = matched
    added.index = data.index
    clashes = [c for c in added.columns if c in data.columns]
    if clashes:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} would add columns named {clashes}, which the '
            f'data already has: set "prefix" to tell them apart, or name '
            f'the columns to add in "columns"'
        )
        raise ValueError(message)
    item.replace(pd.concat([data, added], axis = 1))
    item.record(
        self.name,
        source = (
            'lookup' if lookup is not None
            else str(source) if isinstance(source, str | pathlib.Path)
            else type(source).__name__),
        rows = len(data),
        judges = int(named[_WRITTEN].notna().sum()),
        matched = int(matched.sum()),
        created = list(added.columns))
    return item

def match(
    self,
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    other: pd.DataFrame | Roster,
    *,
    name: str = 'judge',
    court: str = 'court_num',
    year: str = 'year',
    **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
    """Returns the row of a roster for the judge that each row names.

    Args:
        data: the data, with a row for each judge to find.
        other: a roster, or the table of one.
        name: the column of `data` with the judge's name, as an opinion
            writes it. Defaults to "judge".
        court: the column of `data` with the number of the court of the
            row's case. Defaults to "court_num".
        year: the column of `data` with the year of the row's case.
            Defaults to "year".
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `data` lacks one of the columns.

    Returns:
        The position of the judge's row in the roster for each row of
            `data` (see `Roster.match`), or -1 if the name is missing or
            is not matched.

    """
    cases.require_columns(data, [name, court, year], repr(self.name))
    roster = Roster.create(other)
    named = zip(
        data[name].tolist(), data[court].tolist(), data[year].tolist(),
        strict = True)
    found = (
        roster.match(written, _whole(number), _whole(when))
        if isinstance(written, str) and written.strip() else None
        for written, number, when in named)
    return np.array(
        [-1 if row is None else row for row in found], dtype = 'int64')

Bases: Merger

Adds the ideology of the active judges of each case's circuit.

For a case of a court of appeals, the circuit is the court's own; for a case of a district court, it is the circuit of the court of appeals that hears its appeals (see courtpy.courts.circuits). The judges of the circuit are those of its court of appeals in a roster (see Roster) who were active on the day the case was decided: they had been appointed, had not left the court, and had not taken senior status (senior judges do not sit on the court en banc). Their scores are summarized:

Column Meaning circuit_median_party The median party of the presidents who appointed them (-1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican). circuit_total_party The sum of those parties, which is how many more were appointed by Republicans than by Democrats. circuit_median_jcs The median of their Judicial Common Space scores (higher is more conservative). circuit_total_jcs The sum of their scores. circuit_judges How many judges were active.

The scores of the Judicial Common Space are added if the roster has them (make it with Roster.from_fjc(jcs = True)). A judge without a score is left out of its summaries. A case whose circuit or date is not known (or whose circuit had no active judge in the roster) gets missing values.

Like every merger of amos, it never adds, removes, or reorders rows, and records how many rows it matched in the dataset's history. It takes these parameters:

Parameter Meaning source The roster: the path of a saved one, a roster, or the table of one. Without it, the roster saved in "judges" in utilities.data_folder() is used. columns The scores to summarize: "party", "jcs", or both (the default, if the roster has "jcs"). date The column with the date each case was decided. It is "date_filed" unless another is set. court_num, court The columns with courtpy's number for each case's court and CourtListener's id for it. They are "court_num" and "court" unless others are set. prefix Text to put before the names of the added columns. It is "circuit_" unless another is set.

def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    source: Any = None,
    columns: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    date: str = 'date_filed',
    court_num: str = 'court_num',
    court: str = 'court',
    prefix: str | None = 'circuit_',
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Adds the ideology of the active judges of each case's circuit.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of cases (or of votes).
        source: the roster: a roster, the table of one, or the path of a
            saved one. Defaults to `None`, in which case the roster saved
            in "judges" in `utilities.data_folder()` is used.
        columns: the scores to summarize: "party", "jcs", or both.
            Defaults to `None`, for both if the roster has "jcs", and
            otherwise "party" (with a warning).
        date: the column of `item` with the date each case was decided.
            Defaults to "date_filed".
        court_num: the column of `item` with courtpy's number for each
            case's court. Defaults to "court_num".
        court: the column of `item` with CourtListener's id for each
            case's court. Defaults to "court".
        prefix: text to put before the names of the added columns.
            Defaults to "circuit_".
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `item` lacks `date`, or one of `columns` is not a
            score or not in the roster.
        ValueError: if an added column would have the name of a column of
            the data.

    Returns:
        The dataset with the added columns.

    """
    prefix = prefix or ''
    data = item.data
    cases.require_columns(data, [date], repr(self.name))
    roster = find_roster(source, self.clerk)
    chosen = self._choose(roster, columns)
    circuit = courts.circuits(data, court_num = court_num, court = court)
    when = pd.to_datetime(data[date], errors = 'coerce').to_numpy(
        dtype = 'datetime64[D]')
    judges = _active_judges(roster)
    added = {
        f'{prefix}{kind}_{_SCORES[score]}': np.full(len(data), np.nan)
        for score in chosen for kind in ('median', 'total')}
    counts = np.zeros(len(data), dtype = 'int64')
    known = circuit.notna().to_numpy() & ~np.isnat(when)
    numbers = circuit.to_numpy(dtype = 'float64', na_value = np.nan)
    for number in np.unique(numbers[known]):
        rows = np.flatnonzero(known & (numbers == number))
        serving = judges[judges['court_num'] == number]
        if serving.empty:
            continue
        days, place = np.unique(when[rows], return_inverse = True)
        active = _is_active(serving, days)
        counts[rows] = active.sum(axis = 1)[place]
        for score in chosen:
            values = serving[score].to_numpy(dtype = 'float64')
            medians, totals = _summaries(active, values)
            added[f'{prefix}median_{_SCORES[score]}'][rows] = medians[place]
            added[f'{prefix}total_{_SCORES[score]}'][rows] = totals[place]
    table = pd.DataFrame(added, index = data.index)
    table[f'{prefix}judges'] = pd.array(counts, dtype = 'Int64')
    table.loc[~known, f'{prefix}judges'] = pd.NA
    clashes = [c for c in table.columns if c in data.columns]
    if clashes:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} would add columns named {clashes}, which the '
            f'data already has: set "prefix" to tell them apart')
        raise ValueError(message)
    item.replace(pd.concat([data, table], axis = 1))
    item.record(
        self.name,
        rows = len(data),
        matched = int((counts > 0).sum()),
        created = list(table.columns))
    return item

docs.text:
Bases: Converter, Shaper

Makes a table with one row for each judge (Judges).

The rows of each judge in a table of votes (see vote_table) become one row, labeled by "judge_nid" (the Federal Judicial Center's number for the judge), with "judge" (the judge's name), "cases" (the number of the judge's votes), and the means of the columns of numbers and booleans, as group_rows takes them (see courtpy.shapers.summarize). The mean of a boolean is a share: "vote_reversal" is the share of the judge's votes to reverse, "judge_dissented" the share of the judge's cases in which the judge dissented, "type_criminal" the share of the judge's cases that were criminal, "party_type_corporation" (if the parties have types) the share with a corporation as a party, and "judge_age" the judge's mean age when deciding them. Nothing about any one case is kept: columns of text (such as the cases' names and dates) and ids (such as "case_id") are left out, unless "keep" or "how" names them.

If the data is a table of cases (it has no "judge_nid" column), the table of votes is made first, as cases_to_votes makes it, with "roster" and "outcomes".

Like every shaper, it takes "label", "task", and "groups". Without "groups", the table has none, since the groups of votes (such as "case_id") are not columns of it. Without "task", the task is inferred from the label, since a label that was a vote is now a share.

def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    task: str | None = None,
    groups: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Makes the table of `item` a table of judges.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of votes or of cases.
        task: "classify" or "regress". Defaults to `None`, in which case
            it is inferred from the label (see `amos.Dataset.infer_task`).
        groups: names of the groups of the judges. Defaults to `None`,
            for none.
        **kwargs: "label", and parameters for `shape`.

    Returns:
        The dataset of judges.

    """
    dataset = super().apply(
        item, task = task, groups = [] if groups is None else groups,
        **kwargs)
    if task is None and dataset.label is not None:
        dataset.task = dataset.infer_task()
    return dataset

        outcomes: for a table of cases, names of the columns with the
            outcomes of the cases, for which each judge's vote is added.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case they are the columns whose
            names start with "outcome_".
        how: the summaries of columns, by their names, which take the
            place of the means or add columns, such as
            {"court": "list"}. Defaults to `None`.
        keep: columns of text to keep, with the first value of each
            judge's votes. Defaults to `None`, which keeps "judge".
        count: name of the column with the number of each judge's votes,
            or `None` for no such column. Defaults to "cases".
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `data` lacks a column that is needed or named.

    Returns:
        The table of judges, labeled by "judge_nid".

    """
    votes = data if _NID in data.columns else vote_table(
        data, roster, outcomes = utilities.listify(outcomes) or None)
    votes = shapers.add_party_type_flags(votes)
    kept = ['judge'] if keep is None else utilities.listify(keep)
    table = shapers.summarize(
        votes, [_NID], how = how, keep = kept, count = count)
    first = [c for c in ('judge', count) if c is not None and c in table]
    return table[[*first, *[c for c in table.columns if c not in first]]]

Bases: Munger

Adds the judges and the composition of each case's panel.

Each name in "panel_judges" is matched to a judge in a roster (see Roster) with the case's court and year. The judges who are found are listed in "panel_names" (as the roster names them, such as "Lynch, Sandra Lea"), and "panel_found" is how many there are, which can be compared with "panel_size". Each of them also has columns of its own, numbered by the place of the judge's name in "panel_judges": "judge_name1" (the judge's name as the Federal Judicial Center reports it) and "judge_nid1" (the center's number for the judge), "judge_name2" and "judge_nid2", and so on (as add_biography numbers the judges of cases), for as many names as the longest panel lists. A name that is not matched leaves its place missing, so the judges after it keep theirs, and a case with fewer names has missing values in the rest. For each attribute in the roster, "panel_{attribute}" is its mean among those judges: "panel_woman" is the share of the judges who are women, and "panel_party" is the mean party of the presidents who appointed them (-1 for a Democrat and 1 for a Republican). So are "panel_age", "panel_senior", "panel_designated", and "panel_district_judge" (see Roster.describe). A mean is missing if no judge was found (or none has the attribute).

If the cases have "authors", "concurring", or "dissenting" columns, the judges they name are added as "author_name" (the first author found), "concurring_names", and "dissenting_names".

The judges of each case are found as add_biography finds them (see AddBiography), in a table with a row for each judge on each case, and the case gets summaries of its rows (as the merge_summary technique of amos adds them).

Needs "panel_judges", "court_num", and "year".

def munge(
    self,
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    roster: Roster | pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds the judges and the composition of each panel.

    Args:
        data: the parsed cases.
        roster: a roster, the table of one, or the path of a saved one.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case the roster saved in
            "judges" in `utilities.data_folder()` is used.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        The cases, with the new columns.

    """
    cases.require_columns(
        data, ['panel_judges', 'court_num', 'year'], self.name)
    judges = Roster.create(roster)
    described = judges.described
    seated = _named(
        data, 'panel_judges', judges, ['judge', *described],
        unmatched = True)
    panel = seated[seated['nid'].notna()].astype({'nid': 'int64'})
    panels = _summarize(
        panel,
        len(data),
        {'judge': 'list', **dict.fromkeys(described, 'mean')},
        count = _FOUND)
    names = {
        column: _summarize(
            _named(data, column, judges, ['judge']),
            len(data),
            {'judge': 'list'})['judge'].tolist()
        for column in _ROLES if column in data.columns}
    data['panel_names'] = pd.Series(
        panels['judge'].tolist(), index = data.index, dtype = object)
    data['panel_found'] = panels[_FOUND].to_numpy()
    for column, values in _numbered(seated, len(data)).items():
        data[column] = pd.Series(values.array, index = data.index)
    if 'authors' in names:
        data['author_name'] = pd.Series(
            [found[0] if found else None for found in names['authors']],
            index = data.index, dtype = object)
    for column in ('concurring', 'dissenting'):
        if column in names:
            data[f'{column}_names'] = pd.Series(
                names[column], index = data.index, dtype = object)
    for name in described:
        data[f'panel_{name}'] = panels[name].to_numpy(dtype = 'float64')
    return data

def load(
    self,
    source: Any,
    *,
    refresh: bool | str = False,
    scores: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    jcs: bool | str = False,
    martin_quinn: bool | pathlib.Path | str = False,
    rulebook: str = 'judges',
    save: bool | pathlib.Path | str = False,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Downloads the files and returns the table of the roster they make.

    Args:
        source: the folder to keep the files in, or "current" for
            "judges" in `utilities.data_folder()`.
        refresh: whether to download the files even if they are there,
            to get the judges and changes since. Defaults to `False`.
        scores: the path of a file of scores of the judges to add (see
            `build_roster`). Defaults to `None`.
        jcs: whether to add each appointment's Judicial Common Space
            score as "jcs". Defaults to `False`.
        martin_quinn: whether to add the justices' Martin-Quinn scores,
            or the path of the file of them. Defaults to `False`.
        rulebook: the rules that code the judges' careers. Defaults to
            "judges".
        save: whether to save the roster where the techniques look for
            it (see `Roster.save`), or the path to save it to. Defaults
            to `False`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        The roster's table.

    """
    chosen = self._choose(martin_quinn)
    roster = Roster.from_fjc(
        self._locate(source),
        update = utilities.to_bool(refresh),
        scores = None if scores is None else utilities.locate(
            scores, self._get_clerk()),
        jcs = utilities.to_bool(jcs),
        martin_quinn = False if chosen is None else chosen,
        rulebook = rulebook)
    target = self._choose(save)
    if target is True:
        roster.save()
    elif isinstance(target, pathlib.Path):
        roster.save(target)
    return roster.data

docs.title: Roster(data, grace=(lambda: options._JUDGE_GRACE)()) dataclass
docs.text:
A table of judges that finds the judge a name in an opinion refers to.

Each row of the table is a judge's service on one court, so a judge who was promoted from a district court to a court of appeals has two rows, with the president who made each appointment. Only judges who were serving in the year of the case (or had left their court no more than grace years before it) are considered. A name is matched by how much of a judge's name it gives, from the most to the least (see name_forms):

  1. a full name: one of the ways that fjc-biographies writes the judge's name (the "name_..." columns, such as "Sandra Lea Lynch", "Sandra L. Lynch", "Sandra Lynch", and each with any suffix), or one of the judge's "aliases",
  2. or else initials and the last name ("S. Lynch", "S. L. Lynch", "S.L. Lynch", or "S. Lea Lynch"), or the middle and last names ("Lea Lynch", for a judge who goes by a middle name),
  3. or else the last name alone, which is how opinions usually name judges.

The first of them that fits any judge who was serving is used. A name that fits no judge at all is then tried in shorter forms, as a full name or initials (see shorter_names): an opinion's "Susan P. Graber" is "Susan Graber", and its "Ed Carnes" is "E. Carnes", but never the last name alone. Many judges share a name, especially a last name, so the judges whose names fit are then narrowed by the court of the case:

  1. to a judge of the case's court,
  2. or else to a judge of a district court in the case's circuit, who may sit on its court of appeals by designation,
  3. or else to a judge of any other court, such as a court of appeals or district court of another circuit, who may sit by designation.

If more than one judge fits at the first step that any judge fits, the name is not matched, since there is no telling which judge was meant. Nor is a name on a case of a court that has no judges in the table (such as a bankruptcy appellate panel, whose judges are not in the Federal Judicial Center's files), since a judge of another court who shares the name would be a guess.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data DataFrame

the table. It needs the columns "nid" (a number that identifies each judge), "judge" (the judge's name, as it is reported), "last_name", "first_name", "court_num" and "circuit_num" (the numbers that the federal rules give the judge's court and its circuit), and "start_year" and "end_year" (of the judge's service on the court). "middle_name", "suffix", the "name_..." columns that fjc-biographies makes, "aliases" (other names that opinions use for the judge, as "First Middle Last", separated by semicolons), "senior_year", "birth_year", and "court_type" are used if they are there.

required grace int

years after a judge's service on a court ended in which an opinion may still name the judge. Defaults to options._JUDGE_GRACE (as it is when the roster is made).

def describe(
    self,
    row: int,
    court_num: int | None = None,
    year: int | None = None) -> dict[str, float | None]:
    """Returns what is known about a judge on a case.

    Args:
        row: the judge's row of the table (as `match` returns it).
        court_num: the number of the case's court. Defaults to `None`.
        year: the year of the case. Defaults to `None`.

    Returns:
        Each of `described`, as a number (1 and 0 for true and false) or
            `None` if it is not known. "age" is the judge's age at the
            end of `year`, "senior" is whether the judge had taken senior
            status by `year`, "designated" is whether the judge's court
            is not the case's court (so the judge sat by designation),
            and "district_judge" is whether it is a district court. The
            same `dict` is returned each time for a judge, court, and
            year, so copy it before changing it.

    """
    key = (row, court_num, year)
    if key in self._described:
        return self._described[key]
    known = {name: values[row] for name, values in self._values.items()}
    birth = self._numbers['birth_year'][row]
    senior = self._numbers['senior_year'][row]
    known['age'] = (
        None if year is None or birth is None else float(year - birth))
    known['senior'] = (
        None if year is None or 'senior_year' not in self.data.columns
        else float(senior is not None and senior <= year))
    known['designated'] = (
        None if court_num is None
        else float(self._numbers['court_num'][row] != court_num))
    known['district_judge'] = (
        float(self._text['court_type'][row] == _DISTRICT_COURT)
        if 'court_type' in self.data.columns else None)
    self._described[key] = known
    return known

            appointment to the Supreme Court as "mq_first", "mq_last",
            "mq_mean", and "mq_terms" (see
            `fjc_biographies.add_martin_quinn`), or the path of the file
            of the justices' scores ("justices.csv" from
            https://mqscores.wustl.edu/measures.php), which is used for
            `jcs` too. The Martin-Quinn website sometimes refuses
            automated requests, so the file may have to be saved in a
            browser. Defaults to `False`.
        rulebook: the rules that code the judges' careers (see
            `build_roster`). Defaults to "judges".

    Returns:
        The roster.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder).expanduser() if folder else _folder()
    files = download(folder, overwrite = update)
    table = build_roster(
        files['service'], files['demographics'], files['career'],
        scores = scores, rulebook = rulebook)
    named = None if isinstance(martin_quinn, bool) else martin_quinn
    if jcs:
        table = fjc_biographies.add_jcs(
            table, folder, scores_folder = utilities.data_folder(),
            martin_quinn = named, update = update)
    if martin_quinn is not False:
        table = fjc_biographies.add_martin_quinn(
            table, folder, scores_folder = utilities.data_folder(),
            martin_quinn = named, update = update)
    return cls(table)

def identify(
    self,
    names: Iterable[str],
    court_num: int | None = None,
    year: int | None = None) -> list[int]:
    """Returns the judges that the names on a case refer to.

    Args:
        names: the names, as the opinion writes them.
        court_num: the number of the case's court. Defaults to `None`.
        year: the year of the case. Defaults to `None`.

    Returns:
        The rows of the judges who were found, in the order of `names`,
            with each judge once.

    """
    rows: list[int] = []
    judges: set[int | None] = set()
    for name in names:
        row = self.match(name, court_num, year)
        if row is not None and self._numbers['nid'][row] not in judges:
            rows.append(row)
            judges.add(self._numbers['nid'][row])
    return rows

def match(

    name: str,
    court_num: int | None = None,
    year: int | None = None) -> int | None:
    """Returns the judge that a name on a case refers to.

    Args:
        name: the name, as the opinion writes it (such as "LYNCH",
            "R. Thompson", or "Sandra L. Lynch").

            prefer its own judges and those of its circuit. Defaults to

docs.text:
Bases: Converter, Shaper

Makes a table of votes a table of cases again (Cases).

It undoes cases_to_votes: the rows of each case become one row, labeled by "case_id" as a table of parsed cases is, with the case's columns in their order. The columns that cases_to_votes makes for each judge are removed: "judge", and those whose names begin with "judge_", "colleagues_", or "vote_" (such as "judge_party", "colleagues_party", "judge_dissented", and "vote_reversal"). Every other column is the case's, so each case keeps the value of its first row (for votes made from dockets, "case_docket" and "docket" are removed too, and other columns keep the first docket's values). A case with no judge who was found in the roster has no rows in the table of votes, so it is not in the table of cases either. To summarize the judges of each case instead, use code_panels on the cases, or group_rows on the votes.

Like every shaper, it takes "label", "task", and "groups". Without them, a label of votes (such as "vote_reversal") becomes the outcome that it was made from ("outcome_reversal"), and the groups are those of the votes other than "case_id" and the judges' columns.

def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    label: str | None = None,
    groups: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Makes the table of votes of `item` a table of cases.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of votes.
        label: name of the label of the cases. Defaults to `None`, in
            which case it is the outcome that the label of the votes was
            made from, if it was made from one, and otherwise the label
            of `item`.
        groups: names of the groups of the cases. Defaults to `None`, in
            which case they are the groups of `item` that are columns of
            the cases.
        **kwargs: "task", and parameters for `shape`.

    Returns:
        The dataset of cases.

    """
    if label is None and item.label is not None:
        outcome = 'outcome_' + str(item.label).removeprefix('vote_')
        if (str(item.label).startswith('vote_')
                and outcome in item.data.columns):
            label = outcome
    if groups is None:
        groups = [
            group for group in item.groups
            if group != 'case_id' and not _is_judge_column(group)]
    return super().apply(item, label = label, groups = groups, **kwargs)

The files are those of the Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges that are organized by category (see download). The table is the roster that fjc_biographies.build_roster makes, with one row for each court that each judge has served on, and the two columns that courtpy adds to find the judges of cases. Among its columns are:

Column Meaning nid The center's number for the judge. judge The judge's name, as the center reports it. last_name, first_name, middle_name, suffix Its parts. aliases Other names that opinions use for the judge. Added by courtpy. name_first_middle_last, ... The name written in the ways that fjc-biographies writes it, for matching it against other sources. sequence The center's number for the order of the judge's service on the court among the judge's. court, court_type The court's name and its type. court_num The number that the federal rules give a court of appeals or the Supreme Court. Missing for other courts. Added by courtpy. circuit_num The number of the court's circuit: its own court_num, or for a district court, that of its state. start_date, end_date, senior_date The dates the judge's service on the court began (with a commission or a recess appointment) and ended, and the judge took senior status. start_year, end_year, senior_year Their years. end_year is missing for a judge who is still serving. birth_year The year the judge was born. president The president who appointed the judge. party That president's party: -1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican. Missing for other parties. aba_rating The American Bar Association's rating, from 1 (not qualified) to 4 (exceptionally well qualified). Missing if there was none. recess Whether the judge first took the seat by a recess appointment. senate_vote The share of senators who voted to confirm the judge (1 for a voice vote). def build_roster(
    service: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    demographics: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    career: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    scores: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    rulebook: fjc_biographies.Rulebook | pathlib.Path | str = 'judges') -> (
        pd.DataFrame):
    """Makes the table of a roster from the Federal Judicial Center's files.

    The files are those of the Biographical Directory of Article III Federal
    Judges that are organized by category (see `download`). The table is the
    roster that `fjc_biographies.build_roster` makes, with one row for each
    court that each judge has served on, and the two columns that courtpy
    adds to find the judges of cases. Among its columns are:

    | Column | Meaning |
    | --- | --- |
    | `nid` | The center's number for the judge. |
    | `judge` | The judge's name, as the center reports it. |
    | `last_name`, `first_name`, `middle_name`, `suffix` | Its parts. |
    | `aliases` | Other names that opinions use for the judge. Added by courtpy. |
    | `name_first_middle_last`, ... | The name written in the ways that fjc-biographies writes it, for matching it against other sources. |
    | `sequence` | The center's number for the order of the judge's service on the court among the judge's. |
    | `court`, `court_type` | The court's name and its type. |
    | `court_num` | The number that the federal rules give a court of appeals or the Supreme Court. Missing for other courts. Added by courtpy. |
    | `circuit_num` | The number of the court's circuit: its own `court_num`, or for a district court, that of its state. |
    | `start_date`, `end_date`, `senior_date` | The dates the judge's service on the court began (with a commission or a recess appointment) and ended, and the judge took senior status. |
    | `start_year`, `end_year`, `senior_year` | Their years. `end_year` is missing for a judge who is still serving. |
    | `birth_year` | The year the judge was born. |
    | `president` | The president who appointed the judge. |
    | `party` | That president's party: -1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican. Missing for other parties. |
    | `aba_rating` | The American Bar Association's rating, from 1 (not qualified) to 4 (exceptionally well qualified). Missing if there was none. |
    | `recess` | Whether the judge first took the seat by a recess appointment. |
    | `senate_vote` | The share of senators who voted to confirm the judge (1 for a voice vote). Missing if the vote is not recorded. |
    | `woman`, `minority` | Whether the judge is a woman, and whether the judge's race or ethnicity is anything other than white. |

    A judge who was reassigned to another court without a new appointment
    (as when the Eleventh Circuit was divided from the Fifth) keeps the
    president, party, rating, recess appointment, and vote of the judge's
    last appointment.

    If `career` is passed, the judge's career is the column "career" (each
    position on its own line), and each variable that `rulebook` makes from
    it is a column too. The "judges" rulebook of fjc-biographies makes
    "prosecutor", "public_defender", "law_clerk", "supreme_court_clerk",
    "solicitor_general", and "law_professor".

    Args:
        service: the file of federal judicial service
            ("federal-judicial-service.csv"), as a path or a table.
        demographics: the file of demographics ("demographics.csv").
        career: the file of professional careers
            ("professional-career.csv"). Defaults to `None`, in which case no
            careers are coded.
        scores: a table (or the path of a CSV file) with an "nid" column and
            columns of scores for the judges, which are added to the roster
            with the `merge_keys` technique of `amos`. If it has more than
            one row for a judge, the first is used, and a column whose name
            the roster already has is left out. Defaults to `None`.
        rulebook: the rules that code careers: a rulebook of fjc-biographies,
            or the name of one of its built-in rulebooks or the path of a CSV
            file. Its rules search the section "career", which has each
            position that a judge held on its own line. Defaults to "judges".

    Raises:
        KeyError: if a file lacks a column that is needed.
        ValueError: if the file of demographics has more than one row for a
            judge.

    Returns:
        The table, sorted by judge and then by the order of the judge's
            service.

    """
    roster = fjc_biographies.build_roster(
        service, demographics, career, rulebook = rulebook)
    numbers = _number_courts(
        roster.loc[roster['court_type'].isin(_APPELLATE), 'court'])
    court_num = roster['court'].map(numbers).astype('Int64')
    # A court of appeals or the Supreme Court is the circuit of its own cases,
    # as `Roster.match` compares them, so its circuit is its number.
    roster['circuit_num'] = court_num.where(
        roster['court_type'] != _DISTRICT_COURT, roster['circuit_num'])
    columns = list(roster.columns)
    roster.insert(columns.index('circuit_num'), 'court_num', court_num)
    roster.insert(
        columns.index('suffix') + 1, 'aliases',
        roster['nid'].map(_ALIASES).fillna('').astype(str))
    if scores is not None:
        scored = (
            scores.copy() if isinstance(scores, pd.DataFrame)
            else utilities.read_csv(scores))
        cases.require_columns(scored, ['nid'], 'the table of scores')
        roster = amos.mergers.MergeKeys().apply(
            amos.Dataset(roster),
            source = scored.assign(
                nid = pd.to_numeric(scored['nid'], errors = 'coerce')),
            on = 'nid',
            duplicates = 'first').data
    return roster

def clean_name(name: str) -> str:
    """Returns a name the way that names are compared.

    Args:
        name: a name or a part of one, such as "R[obert] Lanier" or
            "O'Scannlain".

    Returns:
        The name in capital letters, without accents, periods, commas,
            brackets, or apostrophes, and with single spaces (as the `names`
            rules of a rulebook write the names they find). Accents are left
            out because sources differ in whether they write them (so a name
            with an accented letter matches the same name without it).

    """
    letters = ''.join(
        character for character in unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', name)
        if not unicodedata.combining(character))
    return ' '.join(_NAME_PUNCTUATION.sub('', letters.upper()).split())

Returns the ways that an opinion may write a judge's name.

Opinions name judges by their last names, with initials or first names only when two judges of a court share one. The forms are grouped by how much of the name they give, which is the order in which Roster.match tries them. For Sandra Lea Lynch, they are:

Level Forms full "SANDRA LEA LYNCH", "SANDRA L LYNCH", and "SANDRA LYNCH". initials "S LEA LYNCH", "S L LYNCH", "SL LYNCH" (as "S.L." is written once its periods are removed), "S LYNCH", and "LEA LYNCH" (for a judge who goes by a middle name). last "LYNCH".

With a suffix, each form is also written with it after the last name (such as "M D SMITH JR" and "SMITH JR"). A form is in only the first level that has it.

Parameters:

def name_forms(
    first: str,
    middle: str,
    last: str,
    suffix: str = '') -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    """Returns the ways that an opinion may write a judge's name.

    Opinions name judges by their last names, with initials or first names
    only when two judges of a court share one. The forms are grouped by how
    much of the name they give, which is the order in which `Roster.match`
    tries them. For Sandra Lea Lynch, they are:

    | Level | Forms |
    | --- | --- |
    | `full` | "SANDRA LEA LYNCH", "SANDRA L LYNCH", and "SANDRA LYNCH". |
    | `initials` | "S LEA LYNCH", "S L LYNCH", "SL LYNCH" (as "S.L." is written once its periods are removed), "S LYNCH", and "LEA LYNCH" (for a judge who goes by a middle name). |
    | `last` | "LYNCH". |

    With a suffix, each form is also written with it after the last name
    (such as "M D SMITH JR" and "SMITH JR"). A form is in only the first
    level that has it.

    Args:
        first: the judge's first name.
        middle: the judge's middle name or names, which may be blank.
        last: the judge's last name.
        suffix: the suffix of the judge's name, such as "Jr." or "III".
            Defaults to an empty `str`.

    Returns:
        The forms of each level ("full", "initials", and "last"), as
            `clean_name` writes them, without repeats. There are none if
            `last` is blank.

    """
    first, middle, last, suffix = (
        clean_name(part) for part in (first, middle, last, suffix))
    levels: dict[str, list[str]] = {level: [] for level in _LEVELS}
    if not last:
        return levels
    written = {
        'full': [
            f'{first} {middle} {last}',
            f'{first} {middle[:1]} {last}',
            f'{first} {last}'],
        'initials': [
            f'{first[:1]} {middle} {last}',
            f'{first[:1]} {middle[:1]} {last}',
            f'{first[:1]}{middle[:1]} {last}',
            f'{first[:1]} {last}',
            # An initial alone is not a name that a judge goes by.
            f'{middle} {last}' if len(middle) > 1 else ''],
        'last': [last]}
    # Without a first name, a full name or initials would be the last name
    # alone, which belongs to the last level.
    alone = {last, f'{last} {suffix}'.strip()}
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for level, forms in written.items():
        for form in forms:
            for written_form in (form, f'{form} {suffix}' if suffix else ''):
                named = ' '.join(written_form.split())
                if not named or named in seen or (
                    level != 'last' and named in alone):
                    continue
                seen.add(named)
                levels[level].append(named)
    return levels

def panel_compositions(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    size: int = 3) -> pd.Series:
    """Returns the composition of each case's panel by its judges' parties.

    The composition names the party of the president who appointed each
    judge, Democratic ("D") ones first: "DDD", "DDR", "DRR", and "RRR" for a
    panel of three (see `republican_appointees`).

    Args:
        data: the cases, with "judge_party1" and so on (from
            `add_biography`) or "panel_party" and "panel_found" (from
            `code_panels`).
        size: the number of judges on the panels to describe. Defaults to 3.

    Returns:
        The composition of each case's panel, as an ordered category from all
            Democratic appointees to all Republican ones, missing for a case
            whose panel is not of `size` judges whose parties are known.

    """
    found = republican_appointees(data, size)
    names = ['D' * (size - r) + 'R' * r for r in range(size + 1)]
    # The number of Republican appointees is the place of the composition
    # among `names`, and -1 marks a missing one.
    codes = found.fillna(-1).astype('int64').to_numpy()
    return pd.Series(
        pd.Categorical.from_codes(
            codes, categories = pd.Index(names), ordered = True),
        index = data.index, name = 'panel_composition')

def republican_appointees(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    size: int = 3) -> pd.Series:
    """Returns how many judges of each case's panel a Republican appointed.

    The judges' parties are those of the presidents who appointed them (-1
    for a Democrat and 1 for a Republican). They are read from each seat's
    "judge_party1", "judge_party2", and so on (which `add_biography` adds to
    cases), or else from "panel_party" (the mean party) and "panel_found"
    (the number of judges found), which `code_panels` adds.

    Args:
        data: the cases.
        size: the number of judges on the panels to count. Defaults to 3.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `data` has neither the parties of the seats nor
            "panel_party" and "panel_found".

    Returns:
        The number of Republican appointees on each case's panel, as whole
            numbers, missing for a case whose panel is not of `size` judges
            whose parties are all known (as for a judge appointed by a
            president of another party).

    """
    seats = [f'judge_party{n}' for n in range(1, size + 1)]
    if all(c in data.columns for c in seats):
        parties = data[seats].apply(pd.to_numeric, errors = 'coerce')
        complete = parties.isin([-1, 1]).all(axis = 1)
        # A panel with more seats than `size` is a panel of another size.
        extra = f'judge_party{size + 1}'
        if extra in data.columns:
            complete &= pd.to_numeric(data[extra], errors = 'coerce').isna()
        counted = (parties == 1).sum(axis = 1)
        seated: pd.Series = counted.where(complete).astype('Int64')
        return seated.rename('republican_appointees')
    if 'panel_party' in data.columns and 'panel_found' in data.columns:
        party = pd.to_numeric(data['panel_party'], errors = 'coerce')
        found = pd.to_numeric(data['panel_found'], errors = 'coerce')
        counted = (found * (party + 1) / 2).round()
        averaged: pd.Series = counted.where(found == size).astype('Int64')
        return averaged.rename('republican_appointees')
    message = (
        f'counting the Republican appointees of panels needs {seats} (from '
        f'add_biography) or "panel_party" and "panel_found" (from '
        f'code_panels)')
    raise KeyError(message)

An opinion may give more of a judge's name than the Federal Judicial Center's files do (as "Susan P. Merriam" for "Sarah Ann Leilani Merriam"), or give a short first name (as "Ed Carnes" for "Edward Carnes"). Such a name is none of the forms of the judge's name (see name_forms), but a shorter way of writing it is: the first and last names, and then the first initial and the last name. A suffix stays with the last name. The last name alone is never one of them, since a name that gives more should not be matched by less than its first name or initial.

the name, as clean_name returns it.

required

Returns:

def shorter_names(name: str) -> list[str]:
    """Returns shorter ways of writing a name that an opinion gives.

    An opinion may give more of a judge's name than the Federal Judicial
    Center's files do (as "Susan P. Graber" for a judge whom the files name
    "Susan Graber"), give middle initials that are not those of the files'
    middle names (as "Sarah A. L. Merriam" for "Sarah Ann Leilani Merriam"),
    or give a short first name (as "Ed Carnes" for "Edward Carnes"). Such a
    name is none of the forms of the judge's name (see `name_forms`), but a
    shorter way of writing it is: the first and last names, and then the
    first initial and the last name. A suffix stays with the last name. The
    last name alone is never one of them, since a name that gives more
    should not be matched by less than its first name or initial.

    Args:
        name: the name, as `clean_name` returns it.

    Returns:
        The first and last names (if the name has a middle name or initial)
            and the first initial and last name (if the first name is longer
            than an initial), as `clean_name` writes them, without repeats
            or `name` itself. There are none for a name of one word.

    """
    parts = name.split()
    tail = 2 if len(parts) > 1 and parts[-1] in _SUFFIXES else 1
    given, last = parts[:-tail], ' '.join(parts[-tail:])
    if not given:
        return []
    shorter = []
    if len(given) > 1:
        shorter.append(f'{given[0]} {last}')
    if len(given[0]) > 1:
        shorter.append(f'{given[0][:1]} {last}')
    return [form for form in dict.fromkeys(shorter) if form != name]

Each name in "panel_judges" is matched to a judge in a roster (see Roster), and each judge who is found gets a row, labeled by the case's id and the judge's place among them (such as "4567890-2"). Cases with no judge who is found are left out. The table is made as amos reshapes and merges data: the lists_to_rows technique makes a row for each name, and add_biography (see AddBiography) adds the judge that each name refers to. The columns are:

Column Meaning case_id The case's id, which the rows of its judges share. judge, judge_nid The judge's name and number in the roster. (the columns of data) The case's columns, repeated for each judge. judge_{attribute} Each attribute of the judge (see Roster.describe), such as judge_party, judge_woman, and judge_age. colleagues_{attribute} The mean of the attribute among the other judges of the panel who were found. Missing if there are none. judge_author, judge_concurred, judge_dissented Whether the judge wrote the opinion of the court, and wrote or joined a concurrence or a dissent. A judge who concurred in part and dissented in part did both. vote_{outcome} For each outcome of the case, how the judge voted: the outcome itself, or its opposite if the judge dissented. So with "outcome_reversal", vote_reversal is whether the judge voted to reverse. Missing if the outcome is.

def vote_table(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    roster: Roster | pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    outcomes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    label: str = 'case_id') -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns a table with one row for each judge on each case.

    Each name in "panel_judges" is matched to a judge in a roster (see
    `Roster`), and each judge who is found gets a row, labeled by the case's
    id and the judge's place among them (such as "4567890-2"). Cases with no
    judge who is found are left out. The table is made as `amos` reshapes
    and merges data: the `lists_to_rows` technique makes a row for each name,
    and `add_biography` (see `AddBiography`) adds the judge that each
    name refers to. The columns are:

    | Column | Meaning |
    | --- | --- |
    | `case_id` | The case's id, which the rows of its judges share. |
    | `judge`, `judge_nid` | The judge's name and number in the roster. |
    | (the columns of `data`) | The case's columns, repeated for each judge. |
    | `judge_{attribute}` | Each attribute of the judge (see `Roster.describe`), such as `judge_party`, `judge_woman`, and `judge_age`. |
    | `colleagues_{attribute}` | The mean of the attribute among the other judges of the panel who were found. Missing if there are none. |
    | `judge_author`, `judge_concurred`, `judge_dissented` | Whether the judge wrote the opinion of the court, and wrote or joined a concurrence or a dissent. A judge who concurred in part and dissented in part did both. |
    | `vote_{outcome}` | For each outcome of the case, how the judge voted: the outcome itself, or its opposite if the judge dissented. So with "outcome_reversal", `vote_reversal` is whether the judge voted to reverse. Missing if the outcome is. |

    Args:
        data: the parsed cases, which need "panel_judges", "court_num", and
            "year". "authors", "concurring", and "dissenting" are used if
            they are there.
        roster: a roster, the table of one, or the path of a saved one.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case the roster saved in "judges" in
            `utilities.data_folder()` is used.
        outcomes: names of the columns with the outcomes of the cases.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case they are the columns whose
            names start with "outcome_".
        label: the name of the column of the labels of the rows of `data`
            (which the rows of each case's judges share). Defaults to
            "case_id". For a table of dockets, it is "case_docket", and
            their "case_id" column is kept.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `data` lacks a column that is needed or named.

    Returns:
        The table, labeled by "vote_id".

    """
    cases.require_columns(
        data, ['panel_judges', 'court_num', 'year'], 'a table of votes')
    if outcomes is None:
        outcomes = [c for c in data.columns if str(c).startswith('outcome_')]
    cases.require_columns(data, outcomes, 'a table of votes')
    judges = Roster.create(roster)
    described = judges.described
    panel = _named(data, 'panel_judges', judges, ['judge', *described])
    origins = panel[_CASE].to_numpy()
    labels = data.index[origins]
    places = (panel.groupby(_CASE).cumcount() + 1).tolist()
    index = pd.Index(
        [f'{row}-{place}' for row, place in zip(
            labels, places, strict = True)],
        name = 'vote_id', dtype = object)
    votes = pd.DataFrame({
        label: labels.to_numpy(),
        'judge': panel['judge'].to_numpy(),
        'judge_nid': panel['nid'].to_numpy()}, index = index)
    numbers = pd.concat([
        panel[described].add_prefix('judge_'),
        _colleagues(panel, described).add_prefix('colleagues_')], axis = 1)
    made = numbers[[
        f'{kind}_{name}' for name in described
        for kind in ('judge', 'colleagues')]].astype('float64')
    made.index = index
    # Whether each judge is one of the judges that each kind of opinion
    # names, which are found in the roster as the judges of the panel are.
    keys = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([origins, votes['judge_nid']])
    for column, role in _ROLES.items():
        made[role] = False
        if column in data.columns:
            acted = _named(data, column, judges)
            made[role] = keys.isin(
                pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([acted[_CASE], acted['nid']]))
    repeated = data.iloc[origins].drop(columns = [
        c for c in data.columns if c in votes.columns or c in made.columns])
    repeated.index = index
    table = pd.concat([votes, repeated, made], axis = 1)
    dissented = table['judge_dissented'].astype('boolean')
    for column in outcomes:
        name = str(column).removeprefix('outcome_')
        table[f'vote_{name}'] = table[column].astype('boolean') ^ dissented
    return table

The sources of court opinions that courtpy can collect and read.

Each module is one source: the CourtListener API (courtlistener), CourtListener's bulk data (bulk), and files downloaded from Lexis-Nexis (lexis). Each can also be imported from courtpy itself (such as courtpy.courtlistener).

base has the classes that the sources build on, which a study can subclass to add its own: a Source reads saved cases, and a Download collects them. Each adds itself to SOURCES or DOWNLOADS when it is defined.

def find_files(self, folder: pathlib.Path | str) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Returns the saved cases in a folder and its subfolders.

    Args:
        folder: the folder.

    Returns:
        The paths of the files that match `pattern`, sorted. Files in
            hidden folders (such as ".courtpy", where downloads keep
            their place) are left out.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder)
    return sorted(
        p for p in folder.rglob(self.pattern)
        if p.is_file() and not any(
            part.startswith('.') for part in p.relative_to(folder).parts))

docs.title: base
docs.text:
Base classes for sources of court opinions and ways to download them.

A Source is a kind of saved case that courtpy can read and parse, such as the JSON files that CourtListener's API and bulk data are saved as ("courtlistener") or the text files of Lexis-Nexis ("lexis_nexis"). A Download is a way to collect cases into a folder, such as from CourtListener's bulk data ("bulk") or its API ("api"), and saves them as one source.

Both add themselves to courtpy when they are subclassed, as amos techniques add themselves to the amos library, so a study can add its own by defining a subclass in a module that it imports:

import dataclasses
from typing import ClassVar

import courtpy


@dataclasses.dataclass
class OpinionsDownload(courtpy.Download):
    # The first line of the docstring is its help in "courtpy download".

    name: ClassVar[str] = 'opinions'

    def download(self, folder, *, courts = None, **options):
        ...

Then "opinions" can be the "download" of load_court_listener and the way of courtpy download opinions. A subclass with the name of one that is already known replaces it. A subclass that lists abc.ABC among its bases is a base class for others, and is not added.

Contents

Downloads

the ways to download cases that courtpy knows, by name. SOURCES: the sources of saved cases that courtpy can read, by name. Download: base class for a way to download cases into a folder. Source: base class for a source of saved cases. find_download: returns a way to download cases, by name. find_source: returns a source of saved cases, by name.

def find_files(self, folder: pathlib.Path | str) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Returns the saved cases in a folder and its subfolders.

    Args:
        folder: the folder.

    Returns:
        The paths of the files that match `pattern`, sorted. Files in
            hidden folders (such as ".courtpy", where downloads keep
            their place) are left out.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder)
    return sorted(
        p for p in folder.rglob(self.pattern)
        if p.is_file() and not any(
            part.startswith('.') for part in p.relative_to(folder).parts))

docs.title: bulk
docs.text:
Extracts cases from CourtListener's bulk data.

CourtListener publishes its whole database as compressed CSV files every three months (on the last day of March, June, September, and December), in a public bucket that needs no API key and has no limits on requests: https://com-courtlistener-storage.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/list.html?prefix=bulk-data/

Five files hold what courtpy needs, and every one is always read, so that each case is put in the court of its docket:

File Size (2026) Holds courts < 1 MB Each court's name and jurisdiction. dockets about 5 GB Each case's court, docket number, and dates. opinion-clusters about 2.5 GB Each decision's parties, judges, date, and status. citations about 130 MB Each decision's reporter citations. opinions about 55 GB The text of each opinion.

BulkData.extract reads them in that order, keeps the cases of the courts and dates asked for, and saves each case in the same form as the API client does (see courtpy.courtlistener), so the same parser reads both. Every case is saved with its whole docket (all of its fields but those in options._DOCKET_SKIPPED), so the dockets file is read twice: first to find which dockets belong to the courts, and again, once the cases are known, to keep the dockets of those cases alone. Reading the opinions file takes hours, so it is worth extracting every court and year you may need at once.

The files are read with amos.loaders.read_chunks, which decompresses and parses them on every core and keeps only the rows asked for. By default, they are downloaded first (to a folder outside of any project, see courtpy.utilities.data_folder) with amos.loaders.download_file and kept, so that they can be used again and an interrupted download resumes. With stream = True, they are read straight from the bucket instead, which needs no disk space but starts over if the connection fails.

Contents

BulkData: lists, downloads, and extracts cases from the bulk data. BulkDownload: extracts cases from the bulk data ("download = bulk"). logger: the module's logger, which reports the progress of downloads and of reading the files.

def available(self, kind: str = 'opinions') -> list[str]:
    """Returns the dates of the files of one kind in the bucket.

    Args:
        kind: "courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or
            "opinions". Defaults to "opinions".

    Returns:
        The dates, from oldest to newest.

    """
    dates = []
    for key in self._list(f'{options._BULK_PREFIX}{kind}-'):
        match = _DATE.search(key)
        # Skips files whose kind only starts with `kind` (such as
        # "opinions-cited" for "opinions").
        if match and key == (
            f'{options._BULK_PREFIX}{kind}-{match.group(1)}.csv.bz2'):
            dates.append(match.group(1))
    return sorted(set(dates))

def chunks(
    self,
    kind: str,
    *,
    columns: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    keep: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None) -> Iterator[pd.DataFrame]:
    """Yields chosen rows and columns of one bulk file, a chunk at a time.

    The file is read with `amos.loaders.read_chunks`, which parses and
    decompresses it on every core and finds the rows in `keep` before
    any of their text becomes Python objects. If `stream` is true, the
    file is read from the bucket as it arrives, without being saved.
    Otherwise, it is downloaded first (or found in `folder`) with
    `fetch`.

    Args:
        kind: "courts", "dockets", "opinion-clusters", "citations", or
            "opinions".
        columns: the columns to return. Defaults to `None`, which
            returns every column.
        keep: the values to keep of each of some columns, such as
            `{'court_id': ['ca1']}` (see `amos.loaders.read_chunks`).
            Defaults to `None`, which keeps every row.

    Yields:
        pd.DataFrame: the rows of each chunk that are kept, with every
            value as text. Missing values are empty `str`s.

    """
    source = self._url(kind) if self.stream else self.fetch(kind)
    yield from amos.loaders.read_chunks(
        source,
        columns = columns,
        keep = keep,
        double_quote = False,
        escape_char = '\\',
        session = self.session,
        timeout = self.timeout)

def extract(
    self,
    courts: str | Iterable[str],
    start_date: str | None = None,
    end_date: str | None = None,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str = 'courtlistener',
    *,
    max_cases: int | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Saves the cases of `courts` filed between two dates.

    Args:
        courts: CourtListener court ids (such as "ca1") or names of groups
            of them (such as "federal_appellate").
        start_date: earliest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None`
            (no earliest date).
        end_date: latest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None` (no
            latest date).
        folder: folder to save the cases in. Defaults to "courtlistener".
        max_cases: most cases to save. Defaults to `None` (every case).
        overwrite: whether to replace cases that were already saved with
            their opinions. Defaults to `False`.

    Returns:
        The paths of the cases saved (or updated) by this call.

    """
    folder = pathlib.Path(folder)
    wanted = utilities.expand_courts(courts)
    date = self.resolve_date()
    logger.info('extracting cases from the bulk data of %s', date)
    court_records = self._courts(wanted)
    docket_courts = self._docket_courts(set(wanted))
    clusters = self._clusters(
        docket_courts, start_date, end_date, max_cases)
    dockets = self._dockets(
        {int(c['docket_id']) for c in clusters.values()})
    citations = self._citations(set(clusters))
    paths: dict[int, pathlib.Path] = {}
    for cluster_id, cluster in clusters.items():
        docket = dockets[int(cluster['docket_id'])]
        court = docket_courts[int(cluster['docket_id'])]
        path = courtlistener.case_path(folder, court, cluster_id)
        if not overwrite and courtlistener.is_complete(path):
            continue
        courtlistener.save_case(path, {
            'source': 'courtlistener',
            'bulk_date': date,
            'court': court_records.get(court, {'id': court}),
            'cluster': cluster,
            'docket': docket,
            'citations': citations.get(cluster_id, []),
            'opinions': []})
        paths[cluster_id] = path
    logger.info('saved %d cases; now adding their opinions', len(paths))
    if paths:
        self._opinions(paths)
    return list(paths.values())
